questions.q: Pain in the right lower quadrant when the left lower quadrant is pressed is called?
questions.e: A classic, if imperfect, sign of appendicitis.

questions.q: Virchow’s node sits where?
questions.e: An enlarged node here can signal abdominal cancer, especially gastric. The umbilicus is Sister Mary Joseph’s.

questions.q: Erb’s palsy affects which nerve roots?
questions.e: Gives the “waiter’s tip” posture. C8–T1 is Klumpke’s.

questions.q: Kussmaul breathing is classically seen in?
questions.e: Deep, laboured breathing that blows off CO₂ to offset metabolic acidosis.

questions.q: Low blood pressure, raised neck veins and muffled heart sounds make up which triad?
questions.e: Points to cardiac tamponade.

questions.q: Cushing’s triad of raised intracranial pressure is hypertension, bradycardia and?
questions.e: A late and ominous sign.

questions.q: Fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot’s triad) point to?
questions.e: Add confusion and shock and it becomes Reynolds’ pentad.

questions.q: Bruising behind the ear (Battle’s sign) suggests?
questions.e: Often appears a day or more after the injury.

questions.q: Carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated (Trousseau’s sign) suggests?
questions.e: Chvostek’s sign, a facial twitch when tapping the cheek, is its partner.

questions.q: Conn’s syndrome is an excess of which hormone?
questions.e: Causes hypertension, often with low potassium.

questions.q: Which organism causes Lyme disease?
questions.e: A tick-borne spirochaete. The classic sign is erythema migrans, the expanding bullseye rash.

questions.q: Koplik spots are a sign of which infection?
questions.e: Tiny white spots on the inside of the cheek, often appearing a day or two before the measles rash.

questions.q: Which bacterium causes stomach ulcers and earned two Perth researchers a Nobel Prize?
questions.e: Barry Marshall and Robin Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize. Marshall famously drank a culture to prove it.

questions.q: “Rice-water” stools are classic for which infection?
questions.e: Vibrio cholerae toxin causes massive watery diarrhoea. Rehydration is the life-saving treatment.

questions.q: Which is the most commonly notified mosquito-borne virus in Australia?
questions.e: Ross River virus causes fever, rash and joint pain that can linger for months.

questions.q: “Slapped cheek” rash in a child is caused by?
questions.e: Also called fifth disease. Usually mild, but it matters in pregnancy and in people with haemolytic anaemias.

questions.q: Q fever is caused by which organism?
questions.e: First described in Queensland abattoir workers. The “Q” stands for query, not Queensland.

questions.q: Australian bat lyssavirus is closely related to which virus?
questions.e: It causes a rabies-like illness. Only vaccinated, trained people should handle bats.

questions.q: Melioidosis, found in tropical northern Australia, is caused by?
questions.e: Lives in soil and water. Cases rise after heavy wet-season rain.

questions.q: Mycobacterium ulcerans causes which skin ulcer?
questions.e: Also known in Australia as the Bairnsdale or Daintree ulcer. Possums and mosquitoes are implicated in spread.

questions.q: What is the smallest bone in the body?
questions.e: About 3 mm long, in the middle ear.

questions.q: What is the longest bone in the body?
questions.e: Roughly a quarter of your height.

questions.q: How many bones are in the adult human body?
questions.e: Babies start with about 300. Many fuse as we grow.

questions.q: Which nerve is the “funny bone”?
questions.e: It runs behind the medial epicondyle of the elbow with little padding.

questions.q: Which cranial nerve wanders all the way to the abdomen?
questions.e: Cranial nerve X. “Vagus” means wandering.

questions.q: Which heart valve has only two cusps?
questions.e: Also called the bicuspid valve. Some people are born with a bicuspid aortic valve too.

questions.q: What is the largest organ of the body?
questions.e: The liver is the largest internal organ.

questions.q: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and movement?
questions.e: Damage can cause an ataxic, wide-based gait.

questions.q: The islets of Langerhans are found in the?
questions.e: They make insulin, glucagon and somatostatin.

questions.q: Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured?
questions.e: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is the clue. X-rays can miss it early.

questions.q: Which ECG change is classic for hyperkalaemia?
questions.e: Tall, tented T waves come first. Then the QRS widens. Then everyone moves faster.

questions.q: The heart’s natural pacemaker is the?
questions.e: The SA node, high in the right atrium.

questions.q: Which coronary artery is nicknamed the ‘widowmaker’?
questions.e: A proximal LAD blockage takes out a lot of the left ventricle.

questions.q: A continuous ‘machinery’ murmur suggests?
questions.e: The fetal ductus that forgot to close.

questions.q: Which valve is most often damaged by rheumatic heart disease?
questions.e: Still common in remote communities. Prevention starts with treating strep throat.

questions.q: Which blood test is most specific for heart muscle damage?
questions.e: Troponin is released when heart muscle cells are damaged, and it’s the key blood test for diagnosing a heart attack.

questions.q: Delta waves on an ECG are a feature of?
questions.e: An extra pathway pre-excites the ventricles, slurring the QRS upstroke.

questions.q: Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation suggests?
questions.e: Often with PR depression and pain that eases sitting forward.

questions.q: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy is also called?
questions.e: Triggered by intense stress. The ventricle balloons like a Japanese octopus pot.

questions.q: What is the most common sustained arrhythmia in adults?
questions.e: AF affects about 1 in 3 people at some point in later life and raises stroke risk around five-fold.

questions.q: What is the antidote for paracetamol overdose?
questions.e: Most effective when given early. It replenishes glutathione.

questions.q: Naloxone reverses which drugs?
questions.e: It can wear off before long-acting opioids do, so people need watching.

questions.q: Warfarin is reversed with vitamin...?
questions.e: Prothrombinex or fresh frozen plasma are used when reversal is urgent.

questions.q: Which antibiotic class can cause tendon rupture?
questions.e: The Achilles tendon is most at risk, especially with steroids or older age.

questions.q: Grapefruit juice raises levels of many drugs by blocking which enzyme?
questions.e: Simvastatin and some calcium channel blockers are classic examples.

questions.q: ACE inhibitor cough is caused by build-up of?
questions.e: Switching to an ARB usually fixes it.

questions.q: Which drug traces its origins to willow bark?
questions.e: Salicylates from willow were used for pain and fever for thousands of years.

questions.q: Digoxin comes from which plant?
questions.e: William Withering described foxglove for “dropsy” in 1785.

questions.q: Which antipsychotic needs regular blood tests for agranulocytosis?
questions.e: Very effective for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, with strict monitoring.

questions.q: Metformin’s rare but serious side effect is?
questions.e: Risk rises with kidney impairment, dehydration and contrast.

questions.q: Which cranial nerve is affected in Bell’s palsy?
questions.e: Bell’s palsy is a sudden weakness of the facial nerve (VII), so the whole of one side of the face droops, forehead included.

questions.q: Parkinson’s disease involves loss of dopamine neurons in the?
questions.e: Literally ‘black substance’.

questions.q: The usual first-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia is?
questions.e: Carbamazepine, an anticonvulsant, is the usual first choice for the stabbing face pain of trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.q: Damage to Broca’s area causes which kind of aphasia?
questions.e: Understanding is relatively spared; getting words out is the problem.

questions.q: Swaying when standing with feet together and eyes closed is a positive?
questions.e: Points to loss of position sense, not cerebellar disease.

questions.q: An upgoing big toe when the sole is stroked indicates?
questions.e: The Babinski sign. Normal in babies.

questions.q: Which antibody is found in most people with myasthenia gravis?
questions.e: A minority have anti-MuSK antibodies instead.

questions.q: A sudden ‘thunderclap’ headache is a red flag for?
questions.e: Worst headache of life, peaking within a minute.

questions.q: Guillain–Barré syndrome typically causes weakness that?
questions.e: Often after a gut or chest infection.

questions.q: Lhermitte’s sign (an electric shock down the spine on bending the neck) is linked with?
questions.e: Lhermitte’s sign comes from damaged nerve coverings in the neck part of the spinal cord, classically in MS.

questions.q: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
questions.e: Australian Howard Florey later turned it into a usable drug, sharing the 1945 Nobel Prize.

questions.q: Who developed the first smallpox vaccine?
questions.e: In 1796, using cowpox. “Vaccine” comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.q: Who pushed for handwashing on maternity wards in 1840s Vienna?
questions.e: Deaths from childbed fever fell sharply. He was largely ignored at the time.

questions.q: John Snow’s 1854 Broad Street pump investigation was about?
questions.e: Removing the pump handle became a founding story of epidemiology.

questions.q: Who discovered X-rays in 1895?
questions.e: One of the first images was his wife’s hand, wedding ring and all.

questions.q: Insulin was first isolated in 1921 in which country?
questions.e: Banting and Best, working in Toronto.

questions.q: Who pioneered the multichannel cochlear implant (the “bionic ear”)?
questions.e: Developed in Melbourne. The first implant was in 1978.

questions.q: Who developed spray-on skin for burns?
questions.e: Used widely after the 2002 Bali bombings.

questions.q: Who co-developed the technology behind the HPV vaccine?
questions.e: With the late Jian Zhou, at the University of Queensland.

questions.q: Who invented the stethoscope in 1816?
questions.e: The first one was a rolled-up tube of paper.

questions.q: Which inherited condition causes iron overload and is common in people of Northern European descent?
questions.e: Usually the C282Y mutation in the HFE gene. Treatment: venesection.

questions.q: Schistocytes (fragmented red cells) on a blood film suggest?
questions.e: Think TTP, HUS or DIC.

questions.q: Haemophilia A is a deficiency of which clotting factor?
questions.e: Haemophilia B is factor IX.

questions.q: What is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?
questions.e: Factor V Leiden is the opposite: it makes blood clot more.

questions.q: Factor V Leiden increases the risk of?
questions.e: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited clotting tendency in people of European descent, raising the risk of DVT and PE.

questions.q: Auer rods on a blood film are seen in?
questions.e: Auer rods are needle-shaped clumps inside leukaemic blast cells and point to acute myeloid leukaemia.

questions.q: ‘Smudge cells’ on a blood film are typical of?
questions.e: Fragile lymphocytes squashed when the slide is made.

questions.q: Howell–Jolly bodies suggest the patient has?
questions.e: The spleen normally removes these nuclear remnants.

questions.q: Which test is used to monitor warfarin?
questions.e: The INR (international normalised ratio) shows how long blood takes to clot. Most people on warfarin aim for 2 to 3.

questions.q: Small red cells, target cells and a normal ferritin suggest?
questions.e: Don’t give iron to fix a thalassaemia trait.

questions.q: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to pioneers of which technique?
questions.e: Announced on 5 October. Switching nerve cells on and off with light.

questions.q: The light-sensitive protein behind optogenetics was first found in?
questions.e: Channelrhodopsin, from Chlamydomonas. Pond life, Nobel-adjacent.

questions.q: Channelrhodopsin opens when it is hit by which colour of light?
questions.e: Shine blue light, and the nerve cell fires.

questions.q: What is the gap between two nerve cells called?
questions.e: Nerve cells don’t quite touch: chemical messengers called neurotransmitters cross the tiny gap, the synapse.

questions.q: Which fatty coating speeds up nerve signals?
questions.e: It's what gets damaged in multiple sclerosis.

questions.q: The light-detecting rods and cones sit in which part of the eye?
questions.e: Their pigment, rhodopsin, is a distant cousin of the Nobel protein.

questions.q: Movement of the left hand is controlled mainly by?
questions.a: The right side of the brain
w: The left side of the brain
questions.e: The wiring crosses over.

questions.q: An EEG records?
questions.e: An EEG uses scalp electrodes to record the brain’s electrical activity, and is key for diagnosing epilepsy.

questions.q: Nerve cells pass a signal to the next cell using?
questions.e: Chemicals such as dopamine and serotonin.

questions.q: Today, optogenetics is mainly?
questions.e: Early human trials exist, including one where a man with retinitis pigmentosa regained partial sight. Still experimental.

questions.q: What do occupational therapists mainly help people do?
questions.e: ‘Occupation’ means anything that fills your day. World OT Day has been held on 27 October since 2010.

questions.q: In healthcare, what does ADL stand for?
questions.e: ADLs are the basic self-care tasks: washing, dressing, eating, toileting and moving around.

questions.q: Which of these is a basic ADL?
questions.e: Shopping, money and phones are ‘instrumental’ ADLs.

questions.q: Carpal tunnel syndrome squashes which nerve?
questions.e: Night-time tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers is classic.

questions.q: A grabber for picking things up without bending is usually called a?
questions.e: A reacher (or grabber) lets you pick things up without bending: an occupational therapist favourite after hip surgery.

questions.q: A walking frame with wheels, brakes and a seat is a?
questions.e: The frame without wheels is the Zimmer.

questions.q: After a right-sided stroke, ignoring everything on the left is called?
questions.e: OTs train people to scan towards the ignored side.

questions.q: Trouble carrying out planned movements, like using a toothbrush, despite normal strength is?
questions.e: In apraxia the muscles work fine, but the brain can’t plan the movement. It often follows a stroke.

questions.q: Grip strength is measured with a?
questions.e: A goniometer measures joint angles. Weak grip also tracks frailty.

questions.q: A raised toilet seat mainly helps people who struggle with?
questions.e: Often after a hip replacement.

questions.q: Which gland is called the ‘master gland’?
questions.e: The pituitary, a pea-sized gland under the brain, sends hormones that boss around the thyroid, adrenals, ovaries and testes.

questions.q: Graves’ disease causes?
questions.e: Often with bulging eyes.

questions.q: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over roughly?
questions.e: About the life of a red cell.

questions.q: Hot flushes around menopause are mainly driven by falling levels of?
questions.e: Most women get them at some point. Hormone therapy and non-hormonal options both help.

questions.q: Too much growth hormone in adults causes?
questions.e: In children, before growth plates close, it causes gigantism.

questions.q: In diabetes, hypoglycaemia is usually treated when blood glucose drops below?
questions.e: ‘Four is the floor.’

questions.q: Diabetes insipidus is a problem with which hormone?
questions.e: Lots of dilute urine. Nothing to do with sugar.

questions.q: Addison’s disease is failure of the?
questions.e: In Addison’s disease the adrenal cortex fails, so the body runs short of cortisol and aldosterone.

questions.q: Iodine deficiency can cause a swollen thyroid called a?
questions.e: Without enough iodine the thyroid can’t make its hormones, so it enlarges trying to keep up. Iodised salt has made goitre far rarer.

questions.q: Which hormone peaks around waking and follows a daily rhythm?
questions.e: Melatonin does the opposite, rising at night.

questions.q: Most strokes are caused by?
questions.e: Roughly 8 in 10 are ischaemic.

questions.q: The World Stroke Organization says your lifetime risk of stroke is about?
questions.e: Today is World Stroke Day, held every 29 October since 2006.

questions.q: In an untreated large ischaemic stroke, about how many brain cells are lost each minute?
questions.e: Jeffrey Saver's 2006 estimate. Hence ‘time is brain’.

questions.q: A stroke in the left middle cerebral artery usually weakens the?
questions.e: And often affects language too.

questions.q: A TIA is?
questions.a: Stroke symptoms that fully go away, usually within an hour
w: A small bleed in the brain
A stroke that only affects vision
questions.e: A warning shot. Same-day assessment matters.

questions.q: Damage to Wernicke's area causes trouble with?
questions.e: Speech flows but makes little sense.

questions.q: Bleeding into the brain tissue is most strongly linked to?
questions.e: Long-term high blood pressure weakens small arteries deep in the brain until one bursts. It’s the biggest risk factor for brain bleeds.

questions.q: Alteplase, the clot-busting drug, is a?
questions.e: It must be given within hours of onset, in carefully chosen patients.

questions.q: A stroke in the back of the brain (posterior circulation) classically causes?
questions.e: Easily mistaken for an inner ear problem.

questions.q: Psoriasis plaques classically appear on the?
w: Elbow creases and backs of knees
questions.e: Also World Psoriasis Day. Severe psoriasis is linked with higher heart and stroke risk.

questions.q: Coeliac disease is triggered by?
questions.e: In coeliac disease, gluten (in wheat, barley and rye) triggers an immune attack on the lining of the small intestine.

questions.q: Tenderness at McBurney’s point suggests?
questions.e: Two-thirds of the way from the navel to the right hip bone.

questions.q: Besides hepatitis A, which hepatitis virus spreads mainly through contaminated food and water?
questions.e: Hepatitis E, like hepatitis A, spreads mainly through contaminated food and water, and can be severe in pregnancy.

questions.q: ‘Coffee ground’ vomit suggests?
questions.e: Blood altered by stomach acid.

questions.q: Barrett’s oesophagus increases the risk of?
questions.e: In Barrett’s oesophagus, long-term reflux changes the lining of the oesophagus, raising the risk of adenocarcinoma.

questions.q: Crohn’s disease can affect?
questions.e: Ulcerative colitis sticks to the colon.

questions.q: A raised lipase is the key test for?
questions.e: Lipase is an enzyme released from an inflamed pancreas. A level over three times normal supports the diagnosis.

questions.q: Gilbert’s syndrome causes a mildly raised?
questions.e: Harmless. Often noticed when fasting or unwell.

questions.q: The low FODMAP diet is mainly used for?
questions.e: Developed at Monash University.

questions.q: Murphy’s sign is used to assess the?
questions.e: Pain stops the breath in when pressing under the right ribs.

questions.q: In 1985 a chemist suggested which rare disease might explain vampire legends?
questions.e: Congenital erythropoietic porphyria, said David Dolphin. Historians and doctors were not convinced.

questions.q: ‘Werewolf syndrome’ is a nickname for?
questions.e: Excess hair growth all over. Clinical lycanthropy is the belief you're turning into an animal.

questions.q: A ‘zombie’ state of staring, stiff stillness and no response can be?
questions.e: It often responds well to treatment.

questions.q: Rigor mortis happens because muscles run out of?
questions.e: Without ATP, myosin can't let go of actin.

questions.q: Goosebumps are caused by tiny muscles called?
questions.e: Left over from furrier ancestors puffing up to look scary.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin works by blocking the release of?
questions.e: This causes a descending flaccid paralysis. Tiny doses are used in medicine.

questions.q: Tetrodotoxin is found in which animal?
questions.e: It blocks sodium channels. One ethnobotanist claimed it was in Haitian ‘zombie powder’, a disputed idea.

questions.q: Cyanide is classically said to smell of?
questions.e: Not everyone can smell it. Rotten eggs is hydrogen sulphide.

questions.q: Methanol poisoning can permanently cause?
questions.e: Its breakdown product, formic acid, damages the optic nerve.

questions.q: The adult skull is made of how many bones, not counting the ear ossicles?
questions.e: Eight cranial and fourteen facial.

questions.q: The prefix ‘nephr-’ refers to which organ?
questions.e: ‘Nephr-’ is Greek for kidney: think nephrology, nephritis and nephrectomy.

questions.q: The suffix ‘-ectomy’ means?
questions.e: -otomy cuts in, -itis inflames, -oscopy looks.

questions.q: ‘Hepat-’ refers to the?
questions.e: ‘Hepat-’ is Greek for liver: hepatitis, hepatology, hepatomegaly.

questions.q: ‘QID’ on a prescription means?
questions.e: Quater in die.

questions.q: The prefix ‘dys-’ means?
questions.e: As in dyspnoea, dysphagia, dysuria.

questions.q: ‘-aemia’ at the end of a word refers to?
questions.e: As in anaemia and septicaemia.

questions.q: The ‘cholecyst’ is the?
questions.e: Chole: bile. Kystis: bladder.

questions.q: ‘Pyrexia’ means?
questions.e: Pyrexia (from the Greek for fire) is the medical word for fever, usually a temperature of 38°C or more.

questions.q: Testing for ‘dysdiadochokinesia’ checks the ability to?
questions.e: A cerebellar sign. Also excellent Scrabble.

questions.q: ‘Stat’ comes from the Latin statim, meaning?
questions.e: ‘Stat’ is short for statim, Latin for immediately. In practice it means drop everything.

theme: Pathology Week: the lab behind the diagnosis

questions.q: In the standard H&E stain, haematoxylin colours cell nuclei?
questions.e: Haematoxylin (from the logwood tree) turns nuclei blue-purple; eosin turns cytoplasm pink. It’s been the workhorse of histology for well over a century.

questions.q: Which white cells are normally the most numerous in adult blood?
questions.e: Neutrophils make up roughly 40–75% of white cells and are first on the scene in bacterial infection.

questions.q: Tissue frozen and cut during an operation, so the pathologist can report within minutes, is a?
questions.e: A frozen section lets the surgeon know mid-operation whether a margin is clear or a lump is cancer. The full report on fixed tissue follows days later.

questions.q: Gram-negative bacteria stain which colour on a Gram stain?
questions.e: Gram-positive bacteria hold the crystal violet and look purple; Gram-negatives lose it and pick up the pink counterstain. Danish scientist Hans Christian Gram invented the method in 1884.

questions.q: HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over roughly the past?
questions.e: Glucose sticks to haemoglobin for the life of the red cell, about 120 days, so HbA1c shows the longer-term picture.

questions.q: Which blood test is the key marker of heart muscle damage?
questions.e: Troponins are proteins of heart muscle. A rise and fall in troponin is central to diagnosing a heart attack.

questions.q: ‘Autopsy’ literally means?
questions.e: From the Greek autos (self) and opsis (sight). ‘Necropsy’ means seeing the dead.

questions.q: Rudolf Virchow, father of modern pathology, popularised the idea that every cell comes from?
questions.e: ‘Omnis cellula e cellula’ (1855). It buried the idea that life springs from non-living matter and grounded disease in cells.

questions.q: Target cells, sickle cells and schistocytes are all abnormal shapes of which cells on a blood film?
questions.e: Red cell shape tells a story: sickle cells in sickle cell disease, target cells in thalassaemia and liver disease, fragments (schistocytes) when cells are sliced up in small vessels.

questions.q: The Pap smear is named after Georgios Papanicolaou. Who was his main test subject for 21 years?
questions.e: Andromachi Papanikolaou let him take a sample from her cervix almost every day for 21 years, which helped him map normal cell changes. Few medical ‘thank yous’ have been more overdue.

questions.q: ‘When you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras’ was coined by?
questions.e: Woodward taught it to students at the University of Maryland in the late 1940s: common things are common. Rare diagnoses have been ‘zebras’ ever since.

questions.q: ‘Cauda equina’, the bundle of nerve roots at the bottom of the spinal canal, literally means?
questions.e: Below the end of the spinal cord the nerve roots fan out like a horse’s tail.

questions.q: Numbness in the ‘saddle’ area plus new bladder trouble is a red flag for?
questions.e: Compression of those nerve roots, often by a large disc prolapse, is a surgical emergency.

questions.q: A ‘charley horse’ is?
questions.e: Usually a painful calf cramp. The origin of the name is uncertain, but it’s been in American slang since the 1880s.

questions.q: The hippocampus, the brain’s memory hub, is named after its resemblance to a?
questions.e: From the Greek hippos (horse) and kampos (sea monster). Anatomist Julius Caesar Arantius named it in 1587.

questions.q: A horseshoe kidney is when?
questions.a: The two kidneys are joined at their lower poles
w: A kidney sits in the pelvis
questions.e: It’s the commonest kidney fusion, in about 1 in 500 people, and is usually found by chance on a scan.

questions.q: Many antivenoms, and the first diphtheria antitoxin, were made using which animal?
questions.e: Horses are given small, safe doses of venom or toxin and make antibodies, which are purified from their plasma. Most Australian snake antivenoms are still made this way.

questions.q: A classic menopause hormone therapy, Premarin, takes its name from?
questions.e: PREgnant MARes’ urINe is the source of its conjugated oestrogens. Women’s health owes the horse more than most people realise.

questions.q: Which animal is the symbol of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and many rare-disease groups?
questions.e: Patients adopted it to say: sometimes the hoofbeats really are a zebra. Rare diseases are rare one by one, but together affect millions.

questions.q: Phar Lap, winner of the 1930 Melbourne Cup, is famous for having a heart that weighed about?
questions.e: About twice the 3.2 kg of an average horse’s heart. It’s on display at the National Museum of Australia in Canberra.

questions.q: What is the functional unit of the kidney?
questions.e: About a million per kidney.

questions.q: eGFR estimates?
questions.e: eGFR estimates how much blood the kidneys filter each minute, worked out from blood creatinine, age and sex.

questions.q: What is the most common type of kidney stone?
questions.e: About three-quarters of kidney stones are calcium-based, mostly calcium oxalate. Drinking plenty of water is the best prevention.

questions.q: Which hormone from the kidneys drives red cell production?
questions.e: Erythropoietin (EPO) is made by the kidneys, which is why kidney failure so often causes anaemia.

questions.q: Adult polycystic kidney disease is inherited how?
questions.e: Adult polycystic kidney disease is autosomal dominant: each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting it.

questions.q: Heavy protein in the urine, swelling and low albumin suggest?
questions.e: Nephrotic syndrome is leaky kidney filters: heavy protein loss in the urine, low albumin and puffy swelling.

questions.q: The kidneys sit in which space?
questions.e: The kidneys sit behind the abdominal lining, in the retroperitoneum, tucked against the back muscles.

questions.q: Extreme exercise, like an ultramarathon, can flood the kidneys with myoglobin from damaged muscle. This is?
questions.e: Myoglobin is toxic to kidney tubules, the CK soars and urine can turn cola-coloured. A modest CK rise is normal after any marathon, such as the New York City Marathon on 1 November.

questions.q: Which electrolyte is the big danger in kidney failure?
questions.e: High potassium can stop the heart.

questions.q: Cola-coloured urine a few weeks after strep throat suggests?
questions.e: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune reaction one to three weeks after a strep throat or skin infection, inflaming the kidney filters.

questions.q: Today is World Tsunami Awareness Day. In START mass-casualty triage, anyone who can walk is tagged?
questions.e: START stands for Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment. Walking wounded go green and are reassessed later.

questions.q: In adult START triage, a breathing patient is tagged red (immediate) if their respiratory rate is over?
questions.e: Over 30, a capillary refill over 2 seconds (or no radial pulse), or not obeying commands all mean red.

questions.q: A limb trapped under rubble for hours is finally freed. The most immediate threat to life is?
questions.e: Potassium and myoglobin flood out of crushed muscle on release. Rescuers start IV fluids before freeing the limb when they can.

questions.q: Bywaters and Beall described crush syndrome and its kidney failure in 1941, in people pulled from?
questions.a: Bombed buildings in the London Blitz
questions.e: Their BMJ paper made the link between crushed muscle and acute kidney injury.

questions.q: Most of the roughly 230,000 deaths in the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami were caused by?
questions.e: The wave hit with little warning. Many victims were women and children, who were less likely to be able to swim or outrun it.

questions.q: ‘Tsunami lung’ is?
questions.a: Aspiration pneumonia from inhaling dirty seawater
questions.e: The water carries mud, sewage and soil bugs, so infections can be mixed and unusual.

questions.q: After floods, which infection spread through water contaminated with rat urine rises sharply?
questions.e: Think fever, muscle aches (especially calves) and red eyes after wading through floodwater. Severe cases cause jaundice and kidney failure (Weil’s disease).

questions.q: The 2004 tsunami was triggered by a magnitude 9.1 earthquake off which island?
questions.e: The quake was off northern Sumatra in Indonesia. Waves reached as far as East Africa.

questions.q: Weeks after big floods in the tropics, standing water often drives a surge in which mosquito-borne virus?
questions.e: Aedes mosquitoes breed in water left in tyres, buckets and rubble. Clearing containers matters as much as clean water.

questions.q: A survivor has a dirty wound and can’t remember their tetanus jabs. The safest plan is?
w: Nothing if the wound looks clean
questions.e: A tetanus-prone wound with an unknown history gets both. Tetanus cases spiked in Aceh after 2004.

questions.q: James Naismith, born on this day in 1861, invented basketball in 1891 in which city?
questions.e: At a YMCA training school, with two peach baskets nailed to a balcony rail.

questions.q: In 1898, Naismith also graduated in medicine from a medical school in?
questions.e: Gross Medical College in Denver, Colorado. He then spent decades at the University of Kansas.

questions.q: In 1892, Senda Berenson adapted Naismith’s new game for women students at?
questions.e: The first women’s college game followed at Smith in March 1893.

questions.q: A ball jamming the fingertip can cause mallet finger, an injury to the?
questions.a: Extensor tendon at the end joint
w: Flexor tendon at the base of the finger
Collateral ligament of the middle joint
questions.e: The fingertip droops. Usual treatment is a splint holding the end joint straight, day and night, for about 6–8 weeks.

questions.q: Jumper’s knee, common in basketball and volleyball, is tendinopathy of the?
questions.e: Pain sits just below the kneecap and builds with jumping and landing.

questions.q: In a rolled ankle (inversion sprain), which ligament is injured most often?
questions.e: The ATFL is the weakest of the lateral ankle ligaments and gives way first.

questions.q: A patient lies face down and you squeeze their calf. The foot doesn’t move. This suggests a ruptured?
questions.e: The Simmonds–Thompson test. A normal calf squeeze points the foot.

questions.q: Commotio cordis is cardiac arrest caused by?
questions.a: A blow to the chest at a vulnerable moment in the heartbeat
w: A blocked coronary artery during exercise
An inherited thickening of the heart muscle
questions.e: Usually a ball or elbow to the chest wall. Fast CPR and an AED save lives.

questions.q: Osgood–Schlatter disease, common in jumping teenagers, causes a sore lump at the?
questions.e: Where the patellar tendon pulls on a growth plate. It settles once growth finishes.

questions.q: Drinking far more than you sweat out during a long event can cause?
questions.e: Low blood sodium can cause confusion, seizures and collapse. Advice now is to drink to thirst.

questions.q: Marie Curie, born on 7 November 1867, won Nobel Prizes in which two sciences?
questions.e: Physics in 1903, chemistry in 1911. She is still the only person to win in two different sciences.

questions.q: The sievert, the unit of effective radiation dose, honours medical physicist Rolf Sievert. Where was he from?
questions.e: He measured doses from radium and X-ray treatments in Stockholm.

questions.q: One gray (Gy) of absorbed dose means?
questions.a: One joule of energy absorbed per kilogram
w: One X-ray photon per square centimetre
One hour next to a radium source
questions.e: Decays per second are becquerels. The sievert weights dose for biological harm.

questions.q: Most external-beam radiotherapy today is delivered by a?
questions.e: A linac speeds up electrons to make high-energy X-ray beams.

questions.q: Proton therapy spares tissue beyond a tumour because protons dump most of their energy in the?
questions.e: Named after William Henry Bragg, who described it in the early 1900s.

questions.q: The superconducting magnet in most MRI scanners is kept cold with?
questions.e: About minus 269 °C, just above absolute zero.

questions.q: A PET scanner detects pairs of photons made when a positron meets?
questions.e: The two photons fly off in opposite directions, so the scanner can work out where they came from.

questions.q: Which radioisotope is used in most nuclear medicine scans?
questions.e: Its six-hour half-life is long enough to image and short enough to fade quickly.

questions.q: ARPANSA says the average Australian gets about how much natural background radiation a year?
questions.e: A chest X-ray adds about 0.02 mSv, roughly a few days of background.

questions.q: Physicist Rosalyn Yalow shared the 1977 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for developing?
questions.e: Radioactive tags let labs measure tiny amounts of hormones such as insulin.

questions.q: Röntgen discovered X-rays on 8 November 1895 in which German city?
questions.e: Working late in his lab. Today is the International Day of Radiology.

questions.q: The first famous X-ray photograph showed?
questions.e: Anna Bertha’s hand, ring and all. She reportedly said, ‘I have seen my death.’

questions.q: Rosalind Franklin’s ‘Photo 51’, key to cracking the structure of DNA, was made using?
questions.e: Taken in 1952 in her lab at King’s College London. Watson saw it without her knowledge.

questions.q: In 1901 Röntgen won the first ever Nobel Prize in?
questions.e: He gave the prize money to his university and never patented X-rays.

questions.q: Who built the first CT scanner, sharing the 1979 Nobel Prize?
questions.e: With Allan Cormack. Hounsfield worked for EMI, the Beatles’ record label.

questions.q: On CT, water is 0 Hounsfield units. Air is about?
questions.e: Dense bone sits up around +1000.

questions.q: MRI signal mostly comes from the nuclei of which atoms?
questions.e: Protons in water and fat, lined up by a very big magnet.

questions.q: Who pioneered obstetric ultrasound in Glasgow in the 1950s?
questions.e: He borrowed an industrial flaw detector from a boilermaker.

questions.q: Marie Curie’s mobile X-ray vans in World War I were nicknamed?
questions.e: She learned to drive so she could take them to the front herself.

questions.q: A ‘double bubble’ on a newborn’s abdominal X-ray suggests?
questions.e: Gas in the stomach and first part of the duodenum, then nothing.

questions.q: Carl Sagan, born today in 1934, popularised the line ‘Extraordinary claims require’?
questions.e: He said it in Cosmos in 1980. Handy in clinic when someone brings in a miracle supplement.

questions.q: The first modern randomised controlled trial in medicine, published in 1948, tested streptomycin for?
questions.e: The Medical Research Council trial in the UK. Randomisation stopped doctors choosing who got the scarce drug.

questions.q: In 1747, naval surgeon James Lind found that which treatment helped sailors with scurvy?
questions.e: One of the first controlled experiments in medicine: 12 sailors, six treatments. Vitamin C was isolated nearly 200 years later.

questions.q: In a trial, the group given a dummy treatment is called the?
questions.e: Comparing against a placebo shows how much of the benefit is the drug and how much is expectation.

questions.q: Side effects caused by expecting to feel bad, even on a sugar pill, are called the?
questions.e: In statin trials, people on placebo report muscle aches too.

questions.q: A 1998 Lancet paper, later retracted, falsely linked autism to which vaccine?
questions.e: The Lancet retracted it in 2010 and the lead author was struck off. Big studies since have found no link.

questions.q: ‘Lunatic’ comes from the old belief that madness was caused by?
questions.e: Latin luna. Studies of emergency departments keep finding no full-moon rush. Night staff remain unconvinced.

questions.q: ‘Influenza’ is Italian for ‘influence’. Whose influence did people blame?
questions.e: Astrologers blamed outbreaks on the stars. Malaria, meanwhile, means ‘bad air’.

questions.q: In 1998, at age 11, Emily Rosa became the youngest author in JAMA. Her experiment debunked?
questions.e: Practitioners couldn’t sense which of their hands was near hers any better than chance.

questions.q: A ‘systematic review’ that pools the numbers from several trials into one result is a?
questions.e: It sits near the top of the evidence pyramid, provided the trials going in are any good.

questions.q: Today is World Science Day. In 1796, Edward Jenner protected a boy against smallpox using material from?
questions.e: It came from the hand of milkmaid Sarah Nelmes. Her cow was called Blossom.

questions.q: In 1854, John Snow traced a London cholera outbreak to?
questions.a: A water pump on Broad Street
questions.e: He mapped the deaths house by house. Most people still blamed ‘miasma’, or bad air.

questions.q: What did Snow persuade the local officials to do?
questions.e: The outbreak was already easing, but the handle became a symbol of public health.

questions.q: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a plate of?
questions.e: Penicillium spores had probably drifted up from a mould lab on the floor below.

questions.q: Fleming worked at which London hospital?
questions.e: His lab is now a museum. Florey and Chain at Oxford turned penicillin into a usable drug.

questions.q: Louis Pasteur’s swan-neck flask experiment disproved?
questions.e: Broth stayed clear while the curved neck kept dust out. Tip the flask and it soon spoiled.

questions.q: In 1929, Werner Forssmann did which experiment on himself?
questions.a: Passed a catheter into his own heart
questions.e: He walked to X-ray to prove it. He was reprimanded, then shared the 1956 Nobel Prize decades later.

questions.q: In 1628, William Harvey used tourniquets on the arm and simple sums to prove that?
w: Blood is made fresh in the liver each day
questions.e: He worked out the heart pumps far more blood than food could possibly make. Galen’s 1,400-year-old ideas were done.

questions.q: Cells taken without consent from Henrietta Lacks in 1951 became the first immortal human cell line, called?
questions.e: They helped develop the polio vaccine. Her family only learned about it decades later.

questions.q: Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray image that showed DNA’s helix is known as?
questions.e: Taken in 1952 by her student Raymond Gosling under her direction. Watson saw it without her knowledge.

questions.q: Which New Zealand-born surgeon pioneered facial reconstruction for WWI soldiers at Sidcup?
questions.e: He’s often called the father of modern plastic surgery. McIndoe, his cousin, led WWII burns care.

questions.q: Archibald McIndoe’s WWII burns patients at East Grinstead called themselves?
questions.e: They were trying new techniques, and they had a sense of humour about it.

questions.q: Which US Army doctor set up the first blood depots, storing blood ahead of battle, on the Western Front in 1917?
questions.e: Landsteiner found blood groups; Drew ran WWII’s Blood for Britain.

questions.q: Napoleon’s surgeon who introduced ‘flying ambulances’ and sorting the wounded by severity was?
questions.e: Triage comes from the French ‘trier’, to sort.

questions.q: In 1537, army surgeon Ambroise Paré stopped pouring what into gunshot wounds?
questions.e: He ran out of oil, used a mild dressing instead, and those soldiers did better.

questions.q: WWI ‘shell shock’ was eventually recognised in 1980 when DSM-III added?
questions.e: Many men with shell shock were treated as cowards, and some were executed.

questions.q: Florence Nightingale showed deaths in the Crimean War with a chart called a?
questions.e: Also called a coxcomb. It showed that infection killed far more soldiers than wounds did.

questions.q: Jamaican-born nurse Mary Seacole ran which establishment for soldiers in Crimea?
questions.e: She sold food and supplies and nursed the sick, often near the front line.

questions.q: Introduced in 1916, the Thomas splint cut deaths from which injury from about 80% to about 20%?
questions.e: Traction stopped bleeding and bone ends grinding. Welsh surgeon Hugh Owen Thomas had designed it decades earlier.

questions.q: Dakin’s solution, used to irrigate wounds in WWI, is dilute?
questions.e: Basically weak bleach. Chemist Henry Dakin and surgeon Alexis Carrel developed it in 1915.

questions.q: The most common bacterial cause of community-acquired pneumonia is?
questions.e: The pneumococcus. Today is World Pneumonia Day.

questions.q: William Osler called pneumonia ‘the friend of the’?
questions.e: Because it often brought a quick, peaceful end.

questions.q: Worldwide, pneumonia is the leading infectious cause of death in?
questions.e: Most of those deaths are preventable.

questions.q: On a chest X-ray, bacterial pneumonia typically shows?
questions.e: Air spaces filled with fluid and pus. Air bronchograms are a clue.

questions.q: Legionnaires’ disease is named after a 1976 convention outbreak in?
questions.e: At an American Legion convention.

questions.q: Legionella longbeachae is famously linked to?
questions.e: Bagged soils and composts carry it. Gardeners, take note.

questions.q: ‘Redcurrant jelly’ sputum is the textbook sign of which bug?
questions.e: Textbooks love it. Real sputum rarely reads the textbook.

questions.q: ‘Walking pneumonia’ is classically caused by?
questions.e: Unwell, but still up and about.

questions.q: In the CURB-65 severity score, C stands for?
questions.e: Then urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age 65 or over.

questions.q: Inhaled material most often ends up in which lung?
questions.e: Its main bronchus is wider and more vertical. Peanuts go right too.

questions.q: Today is World Kindness Day. Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released from the?
questions.e: It travels down nerve fibres to be stored and released, just like ADH.

questions.q: Which hypothalamic nuclei make most of the body’s oxytocin?
questions.e: The same two nuclei also make ADH (vasopressin).

questions.q: Vincent du Vigneaud won the 1955 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the first synthesis of a peptide hormone. Which one?
questions.e: Just nine amino acids, but it was a first.

questions.q: After birth, synthetic oxytocin is routinely given mainly to prevent?
questions.e: Part of active management of the third stage. It makes the uterus contract.

questions.q: A 2010 meta-analysis of 148 studies found that strong social relationships raised the odds of survival by about?
questions.e: Holt-Lunstad and colleagues. The effect was similar in size to quitting smoking.

questions.q: In 2018, which country became the first to appoint a minister for loneliness?
questions.e: Japan followed in 2021.

questions.q: In a 2008 BMJ trial in irritable bowel syndrome, which group improved most?
questions.a: Sham acupuncture with a warm, attentive practitioner
questions.e: Kaptchuk and colleagues showed the relationship itself is part of the treatment.

questions.q: Schwartz Rounds, where hospital staff talk about the emotional side of care, are named after a?
questions.a: Lawyer who wrote about the kindness he got as a patient
questions.e: Ken Schwartz wrote about it before he died of lung cancer in 1995.

questions.q: The #hellomynameis campaign, urging staff to introduce themselves, was started in 2013 by?
questions.e: A UK geriatrician with terminal cancer, she noticed how often staff didn’t say who they were.

questions.q: In 2023, which organisation launched a Commission on Social Connection to tackle loneliness?
questions.e: Around the same time, the US Surgeon General called loneliness an epidemic.

questions.q: World Diabetes Day is held on 14 November because it’s whose birthday?
questions.e: Born in 1891 in Ontario.

questions.q: Banting and Best first isolated insulin in 1921 at which university?
questions.e: Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin at the University of Toronto in 1921. It was first given to a patient in January 1922.

questions.q: In January 1922, the first person treated with insulin was 14-year-old?
questions.e: The other three were famous early patients too.

questions.q: Which Nobel laureate spent 35 years working out the 3D structure of insulin, finally solving it in 1969?
questions.e: She’d already won the 1964 Chemistry Nobel for penicillin and vitamin B12, while living with rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.q: ‘Diabetes mellitus’ literally means?
questions.e: Diabetes is Greek for siphon; mellitus is Latin for honeyed. Early doctors tasted urine.

questions.q: According to WHO, an HbA1c at or above what level can diagnose diabetes?
questions.e: WHO accepts an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or higher as diagnostic of diabetes.

questions.q: Type 1 diabetes is mainly caused by?
questions.e: Not caused by lifestyle. No lolly-shaming.

questions.q: In diabetic ketoacidosis, the breath may smell of?
questions.e: Acetone. Not everyone can smell it.

questions.q: Which test is the standard way to diagnose gestational diabetes?
questions.e: Usually done at 24 to 28 weeks.

questions.q: Charcot foot in diabetes is?
questions.a: Destructive joint disease in a numb foot
questions.e: Neuropathy hides the pain, so a hot, swollen foot can be the only clue.

questions.q: Today remembers road traffic victims. Road injuries are WHO’s leading cause of death for people aged?
questions.e: About 1.2 million people die on the roads each year. More than half are pedestrians, cyclists or motorcyclists.

questions.q: Bridget Driscoll, killed in 1896, is often called the first pedestrian killed by a car. Where?
questions.e: She was hit at Crystal Palace. The car was reportedly doing about 6 km/h.

questions.q: Which Volvo engineer designed the three-point seatbelt in 1959?
questions.e: Volvo left the patent open so any carmaker could use it.

questions.q: A lap belt and a flexion-distraction injury through the vertebral body and posterior elements. This is a?
questions.e: Look for a ‘seatbelt sign’ on the abdomen. Bowel injury often comes with it.

questions.q: Waddell’s triad in a child hit by a car is femoral fracture, chest or abdominal injury and?
questions.e: The bumper hits the leg, the bonnet the trunk, then the child lands on the other side.

questions.q: In the Glasgow Coma Scale, abnormal (decorticate) flexion to pain scores what for motor response?
questions.e: Normal withdrawal scores 4 and extension 2. A small number that matters a lot.

questions.q: A lucid interval then rapid decline, with a lens-shaped bleed on CT, is classically from which vessel?
questions.e: An extradural haematoma, often under a thin temporal bone fracture at the pterion.

questions.q: CRASH-2 showed tranexamic acid saves lives in bleeding trauma patients if given within?
questions.e: The earlier the better. Given after 3 hours, it seemed to do harm.

questions.q: The trauma ‘lethal triad’ is hypothermia, acidosis and?
questions.e: Each makes the others worse. Damage-control surgery aims to break the cycle.

questions.q: The UN’s Decade of Action for Road Safety 2021–2030 aims to cut road deaths and injuries by at least?
questions.e: Speed limits, helmets, safer roads and fast trauma care all help.

questions.q: Today is Mediterranean Diet Day. On 16 November 2010, UNESCO added the Mediterranean diet to its list of?
questions.e: The shared meals, markets and traditions count, not just the olive oil.

questions.q: Which American scientist’s Seven Countries Study put the Mediterranean diet on the map?
questions.e: Keys and his wife Margaret also wrote Mediterranean-style cookbooks.

questions.q: In the Seven Countries Study, which Greek island stood out for very low rates of heart disease?
questions.e: Lots of olive oil, vegetables and legumes, and hard physical work.

questions.q: The main fat in olive oil is?
questions.e: It’s named after olives. Swapping butter for it helps your cholesterol.

questions.q: The big Spanish PREDIMED trial compared a Mediterranean diet with extra olive oil or nuts against?
questions.e: The Mediterranean groups had fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiac deaths.

questions.q: The peppery sting at the back of your throat from fresh extra-virgin olive oil comes from?
questions.e: It blocks the same enzymes as ibuprofen. Not enough to skip the paracetamol, though.

questions.q: In the Australian SMILES trial (2017), a modified Mediterranean diet improved?
questions.e: Led by Professor Felice Jacka. About a third of the diet group went into remission.

questions.q: Which of these is a legume, a Mediterranean staple?
questions.e: Legumes are cheap protein plus fibre. Hummus counts.

questions.q: Which fish is a cheap, oily source of omega-3?
questions.e: Oily fish twice a week is a Mediterranean habit worth stealing.

questions.q: Ikaria, a Greek island famous for living to 90 and beyond, is in which sea?
questions.e: Diet, walking up hills, afternoon naps and lots of company all get the credit.

questions.q: Almost all cervical cancers are caused by?
questions.e: Today is World Cervical Cancer Elimination Day.

questions.q: The Pap smear is named after?
questions.e: A Greek-American doctor.

questions.q: For people with a normal HPV test, WHO recommends cervical screening every?
questions.e: WHO’s 2021 guideline prefers HPV DNA testing over Pap smears, starting at age 30 for most women.

questions.q: To reach more people, many countries now let people screen for cervical cancer by?
questions.e: Self-collected HPV tests are about as accurate as clinician-collected ones, and WHO recommends offering them.

questions.q: The technology behind the HPV vaccine was developed at which university?
questions.e: By Ian Frazer and the late Jian Zhou, in 1991.

questions.q: WHO’s cervical cancer elimination strategy aims for 90% of girls to be fully vaccinated against HPV by age?
questions.e: The 90-70-90 targets: vaccinate 90% of girls, screen 70% of women, treat 90% of those who need it, all by 2030.

questions.q: The WHO elimination threshold is fewer than how many cervical cancers per 100,000 women a year?
questions.e: Australia aims to get there by 2035.

questions.q: Henrietta Lacks’s cervical cancer cells became?
questions.e: Taken in 1951 without her consent. Still used in labs worldwide.

questions.q: Who won a Nobel Prize for showing HPV causes cervical cancer?
questions.e: In 2008. Montagnier shared that year’s prize for discovering HIV.

questions.q: Which two HPV types cause most cervical cancers?
questions.e: About 70% of them. Types 6 and 11 cause most genital warts.

questions.q: In GOLD spirometric grading, GOLD 3 (severe) COPD means a post-bronchodilator FEV1 of?
questions.e: GOLD 1 is 80% or more, 2 is 50–79%, 4 is under 30%. Today is World COPD Day.

questions.q: The BODE index predicts death in COPD. Besides BMI, FEV1 and breathlessness, it scores?
questions.e: Celli and colleagues, NEJM 2004. The E is exercise capacity.

questions.q: Long-term oxygen improves survival in hypoxaemic COPD. The two landmark trials were NOTT and?
questions.e: Both published around 1980–81. UPLIFT and TORCH tested inhalers; ECLIPSE was an observational cohort.

questions.q: GOLD says inhaled corticosteroids help COPD exacerbations most when blood eosinophils are at least?
questions.e: Under 100 cells/µL, benefit is small and pneumonia risk still applies.

questions.q: The emphysema of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is classically?
questions.a: Panacinar, worst in the lower lobes
w: Centriacinar, worst in the upper lobes
questions.e: Smoking-related emphysema is usually centriacinar and upper-lobe.

questions.q: In 1940, before purified penicillin had been given to a single patient, Abraham and Chain described a bacterial enzyme that destroys it, called?
questions.e: Resistance was spotted before the drug reached the clinic. World AMR Awareness Week starts today.

questions.q: The NDM-1 carbapenemase, described in 2009, is named after?
questions.e: New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase, first found in a Swedish patient treated in India.

questions.q: The mcr-1 gene, reported from China in 2015, spreads resistance to which last-line antibiotic?
questions.e: It sits on a plasmid, so it moves between bacteria. It was found in pigs, raw meat and people.

questions.q: The GRAM study (Lancet, 2022) estimated deaths directly attributable to bacterial AMR in 2019 at about?
questions.e: 4.95 million deaths were associated with AMR. 1.27 million were directly caused by it.

questions.q: VanA vancomycin-resistant enterococci swap the cell-wall end D-Ala-D-Ala for?
questions.e: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Lac about 1,000 times less tightly. D-Ala-D-Ser is the low-level VanC trick.

questions.q: ‘NBM’ on a chart means?
questions.e: Nil by mouth means nothing to eat or drink, usually before surgery or a procedure.

questions.q: ‘PRN’ on a medication chart means?
questions.e: Pro re nata.

questions.q: ‘BD’ on a prescription means?
questions.e: Bis die.

questions.q: ‘NAD’ in the notes usually means?
questions.e: NAD means no abnormality detected. Cynics insist it stands for ‘not actually done’.

questions.q: ‘SOB’ in the notes means?
questions.e: Context matters.

questions.q: To ‘turf’ a patient means to?
questions.e: To ‘turf’ a patient is hospital slang for transferring them to another team, ideally without anyone noticing.

questions.q: DNR stands for?
questions.e: DNR means do not resuscitate: no CPR if the heart stops. Many hospitals now use wording like ‘not for CPR’ instead.

questions.q: ‘Obs’ are the patient’s?
questions.e: Obs (observations) are the vital signs: pulse, blood pressure, temperature, breathing rate and oxygen level.

questions.q: A ‘frequent flyer’ is?
w: A patient who needs a flight
questions.e: A ‘frequent flyer’ is hospital slang for a patient who comes back again and again. Best kept off the notes.

questions.q: ‘TTO’ or ‘TTA’ medications are?
w: Medications given at the time of admission
questions.e: To take out, or to take away.

questions.q: Which antiseptic did Joseph Lister use?
questions.e: Phenol, sprayed in the air and on wounds.

questions.q: Who performed the first human heart transplant?
questions.e: Cape Town, 1967.

questions.q: The first public demonstration of ether anaesthesia, in 1846, was in?
questions.e: On 16 October 1846, dentist William Morton gave ether at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston. The theatre is now called the Ether Dome.

questions.q: Who introduced chloroform anaesthesia in 1847?
questions.e: An Edinburgh obstetrician.

questions.q: Which monarch made chloroform in childbirth fashionable?
questions.e: For Prince Leopold, in 1853. John Snow gave it.

questions.q: The red and white of a barber’s pole recall?
questions.e: Barbers once did bloodletting and surgery.

questions.q: The first successful kidney transplant, in 1954, was between?
questions.e: No rejection to worry about.

questions.q: In 1893 in Chicago, Daniel Hale Williams, one of America’s first Black heart surgeons, successfully repaired a stab wound to the?
questions.e: The patient survived. Williams also founded Provident Hospital, which trained Black nurses and doctors when most hospitals wouldn’t.

questions.q: Mary Edwards Walker, a US Civil War surgeon, remains the only woman awarded the?
questions.e: It was taken away in 1917 and restored in 1977. She was also arrested for wearing trousers.

questions.q: William Halsted introduced which item to the operating theatre around 1890?
questions.e: Originally to protect his scrub nurse’s hands.

questions.q: Today is World Hello Day. Brothers Brian and Michael McCormack started it in 1973 in response to which conflict?
questions.e: Their idea: greet ten people and let leaders notice that talking beats fighting. Sadly under-prescribed.

questions.q: In Beckman and Frankel’s classic 1984 study, doctors interrupted a patient’s opening statement after an average of?
questions.e: Eighteen whole seconds. Later studies have not exactly flattered us either.

questions.q: In a 2002 BMJ study from a Basel clinic, patients left to talk uninterrupted finished after a mean of about?
questions.e: The feared endless monologue lasted a mean of 92 seconds.

questions.q: The SPIKES protocol is a six-step framework for?
questions.e: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and Summary. Baile and Buckman, 2000.

questions.q: In the consultation shorthand ‘ICE’, the letters stand for Ideas, Concerns and?
questions.e: Three questions that stop you treating the wrong problem beautifully.

questions.q: Asking a patient to explain in their own words what you just told them is called?
questions.e: If they can’t explain it, the fault is usually in the telling.

questions.q: A 2003 study of paediatric clinics found interpreting errors with clinical consequences were more likely with?
questions.a: Ad hoc interpreters such as relatives
questions.e: Flores and colleagues. Love doesn’t translate dosing instructions.

questions.q: In Rogers v Whitaker (Australia, 1992), a woman wasn’t warned that surgery on one eye carried a small risk of?
questions.e: The risk of sympathetic ophthalmia was about 1 in 14,000. She had asked about her good eye, and consent law changed.

questions.q: ‘Listen to your patient, he is telling you the diagnosis’ is usually credited to?
questions.e: The exact words are hard to find in his writings. The advice holds regardless.

questions.q: Rita Charon, a physician with a doctorate in English, founded which field at Columbia University?
questions.e: Training clinicians to take in patients’ stories as carefully as they read a blood result.

questions.q: Today is 22q11.2 Awareness Day. Roughly how often does the deletion occur in live births?
questions.e: One of the most common microdeletions in people, yet it often takes years to be recognised.

questions.q: The old mnemonic for 22q features borrowed the title of a Joseph Heller novel. What was it?
questions.e: Cardiac, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia. Clinicians and families have mostly retired it, and fair enough.

questions.q: The thymus and inferior parathyroid glands develop from which pharyngeal pouch?
questions.e: Which explains the immune and calcium problems. Inferior glands, third pouch: embryology enjoys being confusing.

questions.q: Which gene in the deleted region is thought to drive many of the physical features?
questions.e: A transcription factor needed for pharyngeal arch development. Mice missing it show very similar heart and arch defects.

questions.q: Which heart lesion has an especially strong link with 22q11.2 deletion?
questions.e: Around half of babies with this rare lesion have the deletion, so genetic testing is routine.

questions.q: About what share of adults with 22q11.2 deletion develop a schizophrenia spectrum condition?
questions.e: One of the strongest known genetic risk factors, and most people with the deletion don’t develop it.

questions.q: Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes involve the same part of chromosome 15. Angelman usually results when the missing copy came from the?
questions.e: This is genomic imprinting. Prader-Willi is the one with the missing paternal copy.

questions.q: French scientist Marthe Gautier did key lab work showing the extra chromosome in Down syndrome. Credit went largely to?
questions.e: She spoke up about it decades later, in 2009. A very old story in science, sadly.

questions.q: Cat eye syndrome, which can include a gap in the iris, comes from extra material from which chromosome?
questions.e: A tiny extra chromosome carrying a duplicated part of 22. The neighbourhood is busy.

questions.q: In 1973, Janet Rowley showed the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia comes from?
questions.e: She reportedly worked it out with photos on her dining table, and proved chromosome swaps can cause cancer.

questions.q: Today’s date, written 11/23, gives the start of the Fibonacci sequence. Which number comes next after 5, 8, 13?
questions.e: Add the last two. That’s all of it, and medieval Italian rabbits never looked back.

questions.q: The ratio of neighbouring Fibonacci numbers closes in on the golden ratio, which is about?
questions.e: Beware anyone who says your navel proves it. The body is less tidy than the internet.

questions.q: Body mass index is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by?
questions.e: A population tool from Adolphe Quetelet in the 1830s, who was an astronomer and statistician, not a doctor.

questions.q: On a fictional chart, a 20 kg child is due paracetamol at 15 mg/kg. That dose is?
questions.e: 20 times 15. Yes, it’s that simple. And yes, people still check it twice, as they should.

questions.q: Adrenaline labelled 1:1000 contains how much per millilitre?
questions.e: One gram in 1000 mL, so 1 mg/mL. Generations of students have been saved by this sentence.

questions.q: A child on the 75th percentile for height is?
questions.a: Taller than about 75% of children the same age and sex
w: Likely to reach 75% of adult height soon
questions.e: Percentiles compare, they don’t grade. Please don’t tell parents their child is ‘only’ 40%.

questions.q: Normal saline, at 0.9%, contains how much sodium chloride per litre?
questions.e: That 0.9% means 0.9 g per 100 mL. Multiply by ten and feel clever.

questions.q: Smoking 20 cigarettes a day for 10 years comes to how many pack-years?
questions.e: One pack a day for one year is one pack-year. Twice the packs, twice the pack-years.

questions.q: In the adult ‘rule of nines’ for burns, one whole arm counts as?
questions.e: Each leg gets 18%. Handy to know, and it adds up to 100 with the groin’s lonely 1%.

questions.q: Virginia Apgar’s newborn score, taken at 1 and 5 minutes, has a maximum of?
questions.e: Five signs, up to 2 points each. An anaesthetist’s neat bit of arithmetic that has saved many babies.

questions.q: In the ABCDE check for melanoma, the E stands for?
questions.e: A spot that changes is the one to show someone. Edges were already covered by B for border.

questions.q: Pityriasis rosea often starts with one larger patch, called the?
questions.e: The rest of the rash turns up a week or two later, right on schedule.

questions.q: Which cells make melanin?
questions.e: People of all skin tones have similar numbers of melanocytes. The difference is what they make.

questions.q: The Koebner phenomenon describes?
questions.a: New lesions appearing where skin is injured
w: A rash that fades with pressure
questions.e: Psoriasis is the classic example. Heinrich Koebner noticed it in 1876.

questions.q: About how many scalp hairs a day is it normal to shed?
questions.e: Your shower drain is not plotting against you.

questions.q: Benzoyl peroxide acne products are notorious for doing what to towels?
questions.e: The acne may improve. The pillowcases will not.

questions.q: Green nail syndrome is caused by which bacterium?
questions.e: It makes a green-blue pigment called pyocyanin. Not paint, sadly.

questions.q: The Fitzpatrick scale classifies skin according to its?
questions.e: Types I to VI, published in the 1970s by Thomas Fitzpatrick to help dose light therapy.

questions.q: In 2020, London medical student Malone Mukwende co-wrote ‘Mind the Gap’, a handbook showing?
questions.a: How clinical signs look on Black and brown skin
w: How to read an ECG quickly
How to prepare for exams abroad
questions.e: Textbooks had long shown rashes mostly on white skin. Patients paid for that gap.

questions.q: Ringworm is caused by?
questions.e: No worm is involved, whatever the name insists. Same family as athlete’s foot.

questions.q: Tooth enamel, the hardest tissue in the body, is mostly made of which mineral?
questions.e: Harder than bone, and it can’t regrow once it’s gone. Do be nice to it.

questions.q: Which is usually the first permanent tooth to come through, at about 6 years?
questions.e: It arrives behind the baby teeth without any tooth falling out first, so many parents miss it.

questions.q: Giving tetracycline to a child before about age 8 can cause?
questions.e: It binds to calcium in developing teeth. Doxycycline binds far less, which is why it gets the short courses now.

questions.q: A child knocks out a baby tooth. Should it be put back in?
w: Only if it’s a front tooth
questions.e: Replanting risks the adult tooth underneath. Adult teeth are the ones you rush to put back.

questions.q: In 1945, which city became the first in the world to add fluoride to its water?
questions.e: Michigan, 25 January. Tooth decay among children there dropped substantially over the following years.

questions.q: In 1866, Lucy Hobbs Taylor became the first woman in the US to?
questions.e: From the Ohio College of Dental Surgery, after being turned down once. Ida Gray became the first African American woman to do so in 1890.

questions.q: In 1844, dentist Horace Wells tested which anaesthetic by having his own tooth pulled?
questions.e: He felt nothing. His public demonstration in Boston went badly, proving audiences are harsher than molars.

questions.q: In 2023, WHO added which gangrenous disease of the mouth and face to its list of neglected tropical diseases?
questions.e: It mainly affects young children living in deep poverty, and mostly in sub-Saharan Africa.

questions.q: George Washington’s famous dentures were NOT made of which material?
questions.e: The wooden teeth are a myth. The real thing was arguably much less comfortable.

questions.q: Which bacterium is the classic culprit in tooth decay?
questions.e: It turns sugar to acid and sticks to teeth. Your toothbrush knows all about it.

questions.q: Today is World Sustainable Transport Day. Jerry Morris’s famous 1953 study found who had less coronary heart disease on London’s double-deckers?
questions.e: Stairs versus sitting. It launched the whole science of exercise and health.

questions.q: Together, outdoor and household air pollution are linked by WHO to about how many premature deaths each year?
questions.e: More than many far more famous killers. It’s just harder to photograph.

questions.q: PM2.5 refers to particles smaller than?
questions.e: Small enough to travel deep into the lungs and, it seems, far beyond them.

questions.q: In 2021, which was the last country to stop selling leaded petrol at service stations?
questions.e: That ended a century of the stuff, invented by Thomas Midgley, who also gave us CFCs. Busy man.

questions.q: In 2020, a London coroner made Ella Adoo-Kissi-Debrah, aged 9, the first person in the UK to have which cause listed on her death certificate?
questions.e: She lived near a busy road and had severe asthma. Her mother Rosamund’s long campaign changed the conversation.

questions.q: WHO recommends adults get how much moderate activity a week?
questions.e: Walking to the bus stop counts. Walking past it counts more.

questions.q: The 10,000 steps target is thought to have started with?
questions.e: A 1960s device called the manpo-kei, or ‘10,000 steps meter’. Harvard’s I-Min Lee later found benefits levelling off well below it in older women.

questions.q: Motion sickness is best explained by a mismatch between what you see and your?
questions.e: Your eyes say the bus is still. Your inner ear disagrees, and your lunch takes sides.

questions.q: In the 1890s, doctors warned women that riding a bicycle could give them?
questions.e: A flushed, clenched look said to be permanent. Oddly, the bicycle went on to do very well for women’s freedom.

questions.q: Victorian train crash survivors with pain and nervous symptoms were often given which diagnosis?
questions.e: John Eric Erichsen popularised it in the 1860s, and it’s often seen as an early forerunner of PTSD.

questions.q: Alfred Nobel signed his famous will on 27 November 1895 in which city?
questions.e: At the Swedish-Norwegian Club. His relatives were, let’s say, not delighted.

questions.q: Late in life, Nobel’s doctors prescribed which substance for his heart trouble, to his considerable amusement?
questions.e: He’d made his fortune taming it for explosives, and called the prescription an irony of fate.

questions.q: The first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, in 1901, went to Emil von Behring for work on?
questions.e: Antitoxin raised in animals rescued thousands of children. Ross and Koch got theirs soon afterwards.

questions.q: The 1949 prize went to Egas Moniz, a Portuguese neurologist, for?
questions.e: Surely the prize the committee would most like back. Later campaigners asked for it to be revoked.

questions.q: Fleming shared the 1945 prize for penicillin with?
questions.e: Florey, an Australian, and Chain, a refugee from Nazi Germany, turned a mould into a medicine.

questions.q: Furious that Best missed out in 1923, Banting split his prize money with him. Macleod split his with?
questions.e: Collip purified the insulin well enough to use in people. Scientific friendships have rarely been quite so tense.

questions.q: Why couldn’t Rosalind Franklin share the 1962 prize given for the structure of DNA?
questions.a: She had died in 1958, and prizes don’t go to the dead
w: She had refused to be nominated
She was not a British citizen
She had already won a Nobel
questions.e: Ovarian cancer, aged 37. Watson, Crick and Wilkins took the medal, and the arguments have never stopped.

questions.q: Who in 1947 became the first woman to win the Physiology or Medicine prize?
questions.e: With her husband Carl, for how the body handles glucose. She had spent years in junior posts despite doing equal work.

questions.q: Julius Wagner-Jauregg won the 1927 prize for treating neurosyphilis by deliberately giving patients?
questions.e: Fever therapy was, astonishingly, an advance at the time. Penicillin mercifully replaced it.

questions.q: Johannes Fibiger won the 1926 prize for showing that a roundworm causes cancer in rats. What came next?
questions.a: The finding turned out to be wrong
w: The worm was named after Nobel
The prize was shared with the worm’s discoverer
questions.e: The tumours had other causes, probably including vitamin A deficiency. Peer review has a long memory.

questions.q: ‘The dose makes the poison’ is a paraphrase of which 16th-century Swiss physician?
questions.e: Water, oxygen and your favourite vitamin can all confirm he had a point.

questions.q: Who is regarded as the father of modern toxicology, author of ‘Traité des poisons’ (1813)?
questions.e: A Spanish-born Parisian chemist who became a star witness in poisoning trials.

questions.q: Prussian blue is an antidote for poisoning with which metal?
questions.e: The pigment traps thallium in the gut. A painter’s favourite gets a second job.

questions.q: Hydroxocobalamin, a form of vitamin B12, is an antidote for which poison?
questions.e: It grabs cyanide to make harmless cyanocobalamin. It also turns patients and their urine red for a while.

questions.q: Calcium gluconate gel is the specific treatment for skin burns from which acid?
questions.e: The fluoride ion mops up calcium in the tissues, which is what makes this burn so nasty.

questions.q: Japan’s itai-itai (‘it hurts, it hurts’) disease, in the Jinzu river basin, was caused by?
questions.e: Mining waste in rice paddies softened bones. Women who’d had many children were hit hardest.

questions.q: Eating unripe ackee, the national fruit of Jamaica, can cause a dangerous drop in?
questions.e: Hypoglycin A blocks fat metabolism. Once called Jamaican vomiting sickness.

questions.q: Alice Hamilton, the pioneer of occupational toxicology, was in 1919 the first woman appointed to the faculty of?
questions.e: She investigated lead in factories for decades. Harvard, in return, kept her out of the Faculty Club and its commencement parade.

questions.q: Agatha Christie picked up her knowledge of poisons working in which job during World War I?
questions.e: Which is why so many of her victims are so pharmacologically correct.

questions.q: ‘Hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter’ describes which toxidrome?
questions.e: Fever, big pupils, dry skin, flushing and delirium. Deadly nightshade could do the lot.

questions.q: The term ‘Siamese twins’ came from Chang and Eng Bunker, born in 1811 in what is now?
questions.e: Conjoined is the preferred word today. The brothers became farmers in North Carolina and raised large families.

questions.q: Conjoined twins are classically thought to arise when one embryo divides later than about?
questions.e: Timing shapes it all. Earlier splits give separate sacs and sometimes separate placentas.

questions.q: Twins joined at the head are called?
questions.e: One of the rarest forms. The Greek word ‘pagos’ means something fixed or joined.

questions.q: In 2009, Bangladeshi twins Trishna and Krishna, joined at the head, were successfully separated at the Royal Children’s Hospital in which city?
questions.e: After more than 25 hours in surgery, and years of careful planning by a huge team.

questions.q: In omphalopagus twins, joined around the abdomen, which organ is most commonly shared?
questions.e: Often the liver, which is partly why imaging and surgical planning take so long.

questions.q: American paediatric surgeon Rowena Spencer argued that conjoined twins arise not from incomplete splitting but from?
questions.e: Her fusion theory challenged the textbooks. She was also a pioneering woman in surgery in Louisiana.

questions.q: On early ultrasound, a dichorionic twin pregnancy shows the?
questions.e: A wedge of placenta runs into the dividing membrane. Monochorionic twins show a T sign instead.

questions.q: Hellin’s law says that if twins occur once in 89 births, triplets occur about once in?
questions.e: That’s 89 squared. It holds surprisingly well until IVF turns up and spoils it.

questions.q: Which group has one of the world’s highest rates of twin births?
w: The Māori people of New Zealand
questions.e: Mostly fraternal twins, celebrated in Yoruba culture. Igbo-Ora is called the world’s twin capital.

questions.q: In twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, the twins share?
questions.a: One placenta, with connecting blood vessels
w: Two placentas joined by a membrane
questions.e: Fetal surgeons can laser the connecting vessels. Very small targets indeed.

questions.q: Today is St Andrew’s Day. If a Scot says you look ‘peely-wally’, you look?
questions.e: Not quite a compliment. A hot drink is usually on the way.

questions.q: To ‘boak’ in Scots means to?
questions.e: Used for the feeling and the event. ‘Gie’s the boak’ means something is disgusting.

questions.q: In Scots, what is your ‘oxter’?
questions.e: Still used by Scottish patients, so it’s a useful one for the ward round.

questions.q: If you’re feeling ‘wabbit’ in Scotland, you’re?
questions.e: Elmer Fudd has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was born in Scotland in 1996. What was she?
questions.e: Born at the Roslin Institute, and named after Dolly Parton, since the cell came from a mammary gland. Scientists’ jokes, everyone.

questions.q: Joseph Lister developed antiseptic surgery while working in which Scottish city?
questions.e: Glasgow Royal Infirmary, 1860s. Patients’ wounds stopped going bad and his colleagues stopped scoffing, eventually.

questions.q: In 1847, James Young Simpson and his friends tested chloroform by?
questions.a: Inhaling it at his dinner table
w: Giving it to a farmer’s dog
Trying it on patients at sea
questions.e: They woke up under the table and declared it a triumph. Do not try this at the Christmas party.

questions.q: Ian Donald got the idea for obstetric ultrasound from equipment used in Glasgow to?
questions.e: He brought tissue samples to a boilermaker’s test site in 1955. Ultrasound’s origin story involves steak and a shipyard.

questions.q: In 1869, the ‘Edinburgh Seven’, led by Sophia Jex-Blake, became the first women to?
questions.a: Enrol at a British university to study medicine
questions.e: Crowds threw mud at them at Surgeons’ Hall. Their courage outlasted the mud.

questions.q: In 2018, Scotland became the first country to bring in nationwide minimum unit pricing for?
questions.e: Set at 50p per unit at first. Studies have since linked it to fewer alcohol deaths.

questions.q: Today is World AIDS Day, which was first held in?
questions.e: It was the first global health day of its kind.

questions.q: HIV mainly attacks which cells?
questions.e: Falling CD4 counts leave the immune system short of its coordinators.

questions.q: Who co-discovered HIV at the Pasteur Institute in 1983, sharing the 2008 Nobel Prize?
questions.e: With Luc Montagnier. She spent decades afterwards working with people living with HIV in lower-income countries.

questions.q: The first drug approved for HIV, in 1987, was?
questions.e: First made in the 1960s as a possible cancer drug, then shelved until it was urgently needed.

questions.q: ‘U=U’ means?
questions.e: With an undetectable viral load on treatment, HIV doesn’t pass on through sex. One of medicine’s best sentences.

questions.q: What does PrEP stand for?
questions.e: Medicine taken ahead of time that greatly lowers the risk of getting HIV.

questions.q: In 1991, the red ribbon was created by?
questions.a: Artists in the New York group Visual AIDS
questions.e: They chose red for passion and blood, and left it free of copyright so anyone could wear it.

questions.q: In 1987, who challenged stigma by shaking the hand of a man with AIDS in a London hospital, without gloves?
questions.e: One handshake, photographed around the world, that helped knock down the myth of casual spread.

questions.q: UNAIDS says what share of all people living with HIV are women and girls?
questions.e: Young women in sub-Saharan Africa are especially affected.
