questions.q: The first medical report of what became AIDS, in June 1981, described a rare pneumonia in five young gay men in which city?
questions.e: Communities organised and cared for one another long before many governments would act.

questions.q: On 2 December 1982, Barney Clark received the first permanent artificial heart, the Jarvik-7. What had his job been?
questions.e: He lived 112 days, tethered to a compressor the size of a fridge. He volunteered knowing the odds.

questions.q: Who performed the first successful open-heart operation using a heart-lung machine, in 1953?
questions.e: On Cecelia Bavolek, 18. He’d spent about 20 years on the machine, with his wife Mary working beside him.

questions.q: Heparin keeps blood from clotting on bypass. Protamine, which reverses it, was traditionally obtained from?
questions.e: Heparin mostly comes from pig gut. Cardiac theatre is more of a farm than it looks.

questions.q: Cardioplegia solution stops the heart mainly using high levels of?
questions.e: The same thing that can kill a heart, used on purpose so surgeons get a still target.

questions.q: What does ECMO stand for?
questions.e: A heart-lung machine for the ICU, running for days or weeks. Perfusionists are the unsung pilots.

questions.q: People with modern continuous-flow LVADs often have what unusual finding?
questions.e: The pump flows steadily, so paramedics have to check other signs. A real curveball for the unprepared.

questions.q: A ‘hybrid closed-loop’ system, sometimes called an artificial pancreas, links an insulin pump to?
questions.a: A continuous glucose monitor and an algorithm
w: A daily blood test by mail
questions.e: Most of the sums get done for you. People with type 1 diabetes have earned the break.

questions.q: Australian engineer Daniel Timms’s BiVACOR titanium heart moves blood using?
questions.e: Just one moving part. In 2025 an Australian man became the first to leave hospital with one, living over 100 days before getting a donor heart.

questions.q: Nina Starr Braunwald, the first woman to perform open-heart surgery, led a team in 1960 that implanted which artificial device?
questions.e: Her valve design was among the first of its kind to replace a human mitral valve successfully.

questions.q: Who first implanted a total artificial heart in a person, in Houston in 1969?
questions.e: It was designed by Argentine surgeon Domingo Liotta and kept the patient going for almost three days, until a donor heart arrived.

questions.q: Today is the International Day of Persons with Disabilities. WHO estimates how many people worldwide have a significant disability?
questions.e: That’s roughly 1.3 billion people. The world’s largest minority, and anyone can join it.

questions.q: Under the social model of disability, what mainly disables people?
questions.a: Barriers in society and the environment
questions.e: Stairs are the problem, the thinking goes, not the wheelchair.

questions.q: The Paralympic movement grew out of games held in 1948 by which doctor at Stoke Mandeville Hospital?
questions.e: A Jewish refugee neurologist who refused to accept that paralysed patients’ lives were over.

questions.q: Each cell of standard braille uses up to how many raised dots?
questions.e: Louis Braille devised it at about 15, adapting a French army code.

questions.q: The ‘curb-cut effect’ describes how?
questions.a: Designs for disabled people end up helping everyone
questions.e: Campaigners in Berkeley fought for ramps, and then along came prams, trolleys and bikes.

questions.q: In 1977, disability campaigner Judy Heumann helped lead an occupation of a San Francisco federal building for almost a month over?
questions.e: The Section 504 sit-in. They stayed until the regulations were signed, helped by meals from the Black Panthers.

questions.q: The word ‘neurodiversity’ is usually credited to which Australian sociologist?
questions.e: Coined in the 1990s from her own experience in an autistic family.

questions.q: Oliver Sacks’s book ‘An Anthropologist on Mars’ took its title from a phrase used by?
questions.e: The autistic animal scientist’s description of how she often felt among other people.

questions.q: A capital D in ‘Deaf’ usually signals?
questions.a: Belonging to a culture and language community
w: Severe hearing loss on a chart
A person who uses hearing aids
questions.e: Sign languages are full languages, and Deaf communities are proud of them.

questions.q: Welsh wheelchair racer Tanni Grey-Thompson won how many Paralympic gold medals?
questions.e: Plus six London Marathon wins. Now sits in the House of Lords, still moving faster than most of it.

questions.q: Today is International Cheetah Day. Unrelated cheetahs famously accepted each other’s skin grafts, because they have very little variation in their?
questions.e: An ancient population crash left them almost genetically identical. Great for grafts, less great for fighting new infections.

questions.q: A survey of captive cheetahs in the early 1990s found chronic gastritis in about 91%. Which bacteria are the prime suspects?
questions.e: Stress and diet are thought to play a part too. The fastest cat on Earth still can’t outrun a sore tummy.

questions.q: Elephants rarely die of cancer despite their size. They carry about 20 copies of which tumour-suppressor gene?
questions.e: Humans have one. Extra p53 helps damaged elephant cells self-destruct: Peto’s paradox, partly solved.

questions.q: Naked mole-rats almost never get cancer. A 2013 study linked this to their tissues being packed with?
questions.e: The super-sized sugar molecule seems to stop cells crowding together. Wrinkly, bald and nearly tumour-proof.

questions.q: A giraffe’s blood pressure is roughly double ours, yet its lower legs don’t swell up. What helps?
questions.a: Tight, thick skin acting like a compression stocking
w: A small pump in each knee
Kidneys that switch off when standing
questions.e: Researchers compared it to a pilot’s anti-gravity suit. Support stockings, savanna edition.

questions.q: Blue blood from horseshoe crabs is used to check injectable drugs and implants for?
questions.e: The LAL test clots with tiny traces of endotoxin. Most crabs go back to the sea after their ‘donation’, and synthetic versions are catching on.

questions.q: Octopus blood is blue because oxygen is carried by?
questions.e: Two of its three hearts pump blood through the gills, the third round the body. Blue-blooded, literally.

questions.q: In 2004 the US FDA cleared which creatures as a ‘medical device’ for cleaning dead tissue out of wounds?
questions.e: Sterile maggots eat dead tissue and leave healthy tissue alone. Leeches were cleared the same year, for a different job.

questions.q: Parrot fever (psittacosis), caught by breathing in dust from dried bird droppings, is caused by?
questions.e: Not just parrots: budgies, pigeons and poultry can spread it too. Polly wants a chest X-ray.

questions.q: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) is most often caught from?
questions.a: Kittens, which carry it more than adult cats
questions.e: Fleas spread it between cats, and young cats usually look perfectly healthy. Cuteness is a known risk factor.

questions.q: Today is International Volunteer Day. James Harrison, Australia’s ‘Man with the Golden Arm’, donated plasma over 1,100 times. It was used to make?
questions.e: Protects babies from rhesus disease. Estimated to have helped about 2.4 million of them, and he famously never watched the needle.

questions.q: Streptomycin came from soil in 1943. Which graduate student isolated it, only for his supervisor Selman Waksman to get the Nobel?
questions.e: Schatz later sued and won a share of royalties, but the prize stayed put.

questions.q: World Blood Donor Day, on 14 June, is the birthday of?
questions.e: He discovered the ABO blood groups in 1901. Before that, transfusion was mostly a gamble.

questions.q: African American surgeon Charles Drew ran ‘Blood for Britain’ in 1940. He pioneered large-scale storage of?
questions.e: He later quit a Red Cross project over its rule of separating Black and white donors’ blood. Science had no such rule.

questions.q: Which blood group is the universal plasma donor?
questions.e: AB plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies. O negative takes the red cell prize.

questions.q: Vancomycin came from soil collected by a missionary, who sent it to Eli Lilly from?
questions.e: Volunteers really will post anything. The bug inside produced a last-line antibiotic.

questions.q: Rapamycin (sirolimus) gets its name from soil gathered on?
questions.e: Rapa Nui is Easter Island’s Polynesian name. A 1964 Canadian expedition came back with some very useful dirt.

questions.q: The 1803 Balmis Expedition carried smallpox vaccine from Spain to the Americas by?
questions.a: Passing it arm to arm among orphan boys
questions.e: Nurse Isabel Zendal cared for the boys. WHO has called her the first nurse in international mission.

questions.q: In 1901, US Army nurse Clara Maass died after volunteering to be bitten by mosquitoes in Havana, to study?
questions.e: She was 25. Public shock helped end this kind of experiment on people.

questions.q: In 1974, Shirley Nolan, searching for a match for her son Anthony, founded the world’s first?
questions.e: Anthony died in 1979. The register she started has saved thousands of lives.

questions.q: Today is Finland’s Independence Day. In Finnish, ‘krapula’ means?
questions.e: Finnish has a lot of words worth knowing, and this one is particularly useful in January.

questions.q: Finnish patients usually head to a ‘terveyskeskus’. That’s a?
questions.e: Literally ‘health centre’. The heart of Finnish primary care, and a long word for a tired receptionist.

questions.q: Sápmi, the homeland of the Sámi people, spans Finland, Norway, Sweden and?
questions.e: The only Indigenous people recognised in the EU, with their own parliaments in three Nordic countries.

questions.q: Which doctor led Finland’s North Karelia Project from 1972, a famous community effort against heart disease?
questions.e: Heart disease deaths in the region fell dramatically. Butter was the main casualty.

questions.q: Xylitol, studied in the Turku sugar trials for tooth decay in the 1970s, was first made commercially in Finland from?
questions.e: Hence ‘birch sugar’. Finnish children chew it in gum; your dog must not.

questions.q: The ‘Finnish disease heritage’ of about 36 rare inherited diseases is mainly explained by?
questions.a: A founder effect and genetic isolation
questions.e: A small founding population, then centuries of limited mixing. Whereas cystic fibrosis is unusually rare there.

questions.q: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type is caused by mutations affecting which kidney protein?
questions.e: Part of the slit diaphragm of the glomerular filter. Karl Tryggvason’s team found the gene in 1998.

questions.q: Which hantavirus, carried by bank voles and causing a mild kidney fever, is named after a Finnish municipality?
questions.e: Nephropathia epidemica, known to many Finns from cleaning the summer cottage.

questions.q: Since 1938, Finland has offered new mothers a maternity package. The box itself famously doubles as?
questions.e: Originally for low-income families, then opened to all in 1949. Copied around the world.

questions.q: A 2015 study of men in Kuopio found those using a sauna 4 to 7 times a week had a lower risk of?
questions.e: Observational, and only men, so it may just be that the sort of person who saunas is relaxed about everything.

questions.q: Today is International Civil Aviation Day. Ears pop on a plane as pressure equalises through the?
questions.e: Swallowing or yawning opens it. Crying babies are, annoyingly, doing this right.

questions.q: Which direction of flight usually causes worse jet lag?
questions.e: The body clock would rather stay up late than go to bed early.

questions.q: Blowing gently against a pinched nose to clear your ears is named after which Italian anatomist?
questions.e: Eustachi got the tube, Valsalva got the manoeuvre, Falloppio went elsewhere entirely.

questions.q: Passenger cabins are pressurised to the equivalent of about what altitude?
questions.e: That’s around 8,000 feet, enough to make your chip bag swell and your drink hit harder. Sort of.

questions.q: ‘Economy class syndrome’ is a nickname for?
questions.e: Long stretches of sitting, not your ticket. Business class gets clots too.

questions.q: Which Reverend founded Australia’s flying doctor service, which took to the air in 1928?
questions.e: Now the Royal Flying Doctor Service, bringing care to remote communities across a whole continent.

questions.q: In 1930, the first female airline flight attendant, Ellen Church, was trained as a?
questions.e: She wanted to fly the plane. The airline said no, but agreed that a nurse aboard might calm passengers.

questions.q: The way gas in your gut or middle ear expands as cabin pressure falls is explained by?
questions.e: Lower pressure, bigger volume. Which is why bloating on long flights isn’t just that second helping.

questions.q: Which hormone from the pineal gland helps set the body clock and is often linked to jet lag?
questions.e: It rises in darkness. It’s also why the sun at your destination matters so much.

questions.q: Amelia Earhart worked in which role in Toronto during World War I?
questions.e: Treating wounded soldiers, then the 1918 flu, before she got anywhere near a cockpit.

questions.q: The ‘Rx’ at the top of a prescription comes from the Latin for?
questions.e: ‘Recipe’ meant ‘take this’. So it’s a recipe after all.

questions.q: The Bowl of Hygieia, a symbol of pharmacy, shows a bowl and a?
questions.e: Hygieia was the Greek goddess of health, and her name gave us hygiene.

questions.q: Which fizzy drink was invented in 1886 by Atlanta pharmacist John Pemberton?
questions.e: Sold first as a patent medicine for headaches and nerves. Fine, Dr Pepper was also a pharmacist’s, but not his.

questions.q: Gertrude Elion won a 1988 Nobel Prize without a doctorate. Her team’s work led to which antiviral?
questions.e: She gave up on a PhD to keep her lab job. It seems to have worked out.

questions.q: Frances Kelsey at the US FDA famously refused to approve which drug in the early 1960s?
questions.e: Her doubts spared countless American families. Her reward was a President’s medal and a lot of angry drug reps.

questions.q: In the US, paracetamol is known as?
questions.e: Same drug, different passport. Handy to know when you’re travelling.

questions.q: An ‘enteric-coated’ tablet is designed to?
questions.a: Dissolve in the intestine rather than the stomach
questions.e: Crushing it defeats the point, so don’t, unless your pharmacist says you can.

questions.q: Which society let Elizabeth Garrett Anderson qualify as a doctor in Britain in 1865?
questions.e: Their charter said ‘persons’, and she was one. They soon changed the rules to stop anyone else trying it.

questions.q: In 1977, WHO first published which list?
questions.a: The Model List of Essential Medicines
questions.e: About 200 drugs at first, and updated every two years ever since.

questions.q: ‘Sublingual’ means a medicine goes?
questions.e: Quick to absorb, bypassing the gut and first pass through the liver. Glyceryl trinitrate is a classic.

questions.q: Which jellyfish sting is treated with vinegar in tropical Australia?
questions.e: Vinegar stops unfired stinging cells going off. Urine remains a terrible idea, however close at hand.

questions.q: Entomologist Justin Schmidt’s famous sting pain index gave its top rating to which insect?
questions.e: Stung about a thousand times over his career, he described each pain like a fine wine.

questions.q: In 1961, how did Dr Jack Barnes prove a tiny jellyfish caused Irukandji syndrome?
questions.a: He stung himself, his son and a lifeguard
w: He tested the venom on mice
questions.e: All three ended up in hospital. The jellyfish became Carukia barnesi, which seems fair.

questions.q: Which egg-laying mammal delivers venom from a spur on the male’s hind leg?
questions.e: Excruciating pain, and morphine barely helps. Cute is no guarantee of anything.

questions.q: Australian funnel-web spider antivenom, available since 1981, is raised in?
questions.e: Milked by hand, spider by spider. There have been no recorded deaths from their bite since it arrived.

questions.q: Who developed the first snake antivenom in the 1890s, after cobra bites in Vietnam drew his attention?
questions.e: Saigon, working for Pasteur. He also gave his name to the C in BCG.

questions.q: In 2017, WHO added which problem to its list of highest-priority neglected tropical diseases?
questions.e: It kills up to about 138,000 people a year, mostly poor rural workers in Asia and Africa.

questions.q: Captopril, the first ACE inhibitor, was developed from the venom of which Brazilian snake?
questions.e: Brazilian researcher Sérgio Ferreira studied the venom that dropped blood pressure. Bitten banana plantation workers had long been known to collapse.

questions.q: The diabetes drug exenatide comes from a hormone first found in the saliva of which animal?
questions.e: A lizard that goes months between meals. Nature’s GLP-1 was there long before the headlines.

questions.q: Sydney allergist Sharon van Nunen linked tick bites to an allergy to?
questions.e: Her work helped put this on the world map. People with the alpha-gal allergy can react hours after eating a steak.

questions.q: The Nobel ceremonies are held every 10 December because that date marks?
w: The founding of the Nobel Foundation
questions.e: He died in San Remo in 1896. The Peace Prize is handed out in Oslo on the same day.

questions.q: Which body chooses the Physiology or Medicine laureates?
questions.a: The Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute
w: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences
questions.e: Fifty Karolinska professors. The other bodies get chemistry, physics, literature and peace.

questions.q: Barbara McClintock won the 1983 prize, unshared, for discovering ‘jumping genes’ in?
questions.e: Her colleagues ignored her for decades. She carried on with the corn.

questions.q: Tu Youyou won the 2015 prize for artemisinin, a malaria drug she found in?
questions.e: She tried an ancient Chinese recipe, and tested the extract on herself first. The first Chinese woman to win any Nobel Prize.

questions.q: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman won the 2023 prize for work that made possible which kind of vaccine?
questions.e: She was once demoted at her university over this research. Sweet revenge, Stockholm style.

questions.q: Camillo Golgi and Santiago Ramón y Cajal shared the 1906 prize, while disagreeing about?
questions.e: Cajal was right. Golgi argued against him in his own Nobel lecture. Awkward Swedish banquet.

questions.q: Rita Levi-Montalcini, forced out of her university post by Italy’s racial laws, began her famous work in?
questions.e: Using chick embryos and sewing needles. She won in 1986 for nerve growth factor and lived to 103.

questions.q: Tasmanian-born Elizabeth Blackburn shared the 2009 prize with Carol Greider and Jack Szostak for work on?
questions.e: The caps on your chromosomes. Also the first time two women shared the medicine prize.

questions.q: Congolese gynaecologist Denis Mukwege shared the 2018 Peace Prize for?
questions.a: Treating survivors of wartime sexual violence
questions.e: At Panzi Hospital in Bukavu. He shared it with Nadia Murad, a survivor and campaigner.

questions.q: Ivan Pavlov’s 1904 Nobel Prize was for his work on?
questions.e: Not the bell. The dogs were part of the digestive project first. Everyone gets this wrong, so you’re in fine company.

questions.q: Today is International Mountain Day. Altitude sickness usually becomes a risk above about?
questions.e: A lot of ski resorts sit right on the line.

questions.q: Which scoring system is best known for assessing acute mountain sickness?
questions.e: Named after the Canadian resort that hosted the meeting. Not a bad spot for a consensus.

questions.q: High altitude pulmonary oedema is mainly caused by?
questions.e: The lungs’ blood vessels clamp down, and fluid is pushed through. A non-cardiac cause of very wet lungs.

questions.q: Acetazolamide, used to prevent altitude sickness, is a?
questions.e: Pushes up your breathing by making the blood a bit more acid.

questions.q: Does being fit protect against altitude sickness?
questions.e: Fit people tend to go up faster, which rather makes things worse.

questions.q: Who in 1975 became the first woman to summit Everest?
questions.e: From Japan, after surviving an avalanche on the same climb. She had raised funds by giving piano lessons.

questions.q: The EPAS1 gene variant that protects many Tibetans at altitude seems to have come from?
questions.e: Ancient interbreeding handed down a very useful adaptation.

questions.q: In the 2009 Caudwell Xtreme Everest study, arterial blood taken near the summit had a mean oxygen level of about?
questions.e: Grocott and colleagues drew it themselves, high on the mountain. Normal is around 90 to 100.

questions.q: Chronic mountain sickness, with too many red cells, is also called which Peruvian doctor’s disease?
questions.e: Carlos Monge described it in the Andes in the 1920s. Carrión has his own Peruvian fever.

questions.q: At altitude, people commonly experience which odd sleeping pattern?
questions.e: Breathing swings between deep and shallow, in the same style as Cheyne-Stokes. Alarming for tent-mates.

questions.q: Today is Universal Health Coverage Day. The 1978 Declaration of Alma-Ata on primary health care was agreed in what is now?
questions.e: The city is now called Almaty. Soviet hospitality, serious ambitions.

questions.q: The Alma-Ata Declaration called for ‘Health for All’ by the year?
questions.e: An ambitious deadline that came and went. The goal itself is still around.

questions.q: Which town’s mutual aid society did Aneurin Bevan say was the model for Britain’s NHS?
questions.e: Miners paid into a fund for doctors in his Welsh home town. He just took it national.

questions.q: Which country introduced the first national social health insurance, under Bismarck, in 1883?
questions.e: He wasn’t being kind. It was a clever way to take the air out of socialists’ sails.

questions.q: Tommy Douglas, voted the Greatest Canadian in 2004, brought in Canada’s first public medical insurance in which province?
questions.e: In 1962, against a doctors’ strike. He also happens to be the grandfather of actor Kiefer Sutherland.

questions.q: Who proposed the ‘inverse care law’ in The Lancet in 1971?
questions.e: A rule from a GP in a Welsh mining village: those who need good care most are least likely to get it. Still depressingly current.

questions.q: The ‘Beveridge’ model of health system is funded mainly by?
questions.e: Think UK, Spain or New Zealand. Bismarck’s model uses insurance funds instead.

questions.q: Thailand’s universal coverage scheme, launched in 2001 to 2002, was known by its patient fee of?
questions.e: Under a dollar a visit. A middle-income country showing big budgets aren’t the only way.

questions.q: WHO and the World Bank say about what share of the world lacked full access to essential health services in 2021?
questions.e: Around 4.5 billion people. Some 2 billion faced financial hardship from care costs too.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to lead the World Health Organization, from 1998?
questions.e: A doctor and Norway’s former prime minister. She went straight after tobacco.

questions.q: On this date in 1947, JAMA published Claude Beck’s report of the first successful defibrillation of a human heart. The patient was?
w: A man collapsing in the street
A newborn in a delivery room
questions.e: In Cleveland, with paddles held directly on the open heart and a home-built machine. The boy recovered fully.

questions.q: Which two Geneva physiologists showed in 1899 that electric shocks could stop ventricular fibrillation in dogs?
questions.e: The idea then sat largely ignored for about half a century, which is a long time to leave a good idea on hold.

questions.q: Belfast cardiologist Frank Pantridge changed emergency care in the 1960s by?
questions.a: Putting a portable defibrillator in an ambulance
questions.e: His first version ran on car batteries. A statue of him stands in Lisburn.

questions.q: Commotio cordis is sudden cardiac arrest from a blow to the chest timed to?
questions.a: The upstroke of the T wave
questions.e: A tiny vulnerable window of a few tens of milliseconds. It happens mostly in young athletes, and takes astonishing bad luck.

questions.q: Bernard Lown made a major advance in the early 1960s with?
questions.a: The DC defibrillator and synchronised cardioversion
questions.e: Direct current turned out far safer than AC. He also co-founded the group that won the 1985 Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.q: Who led the development of the implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, first used in a patient in 1980?
questions.e: Many colleagues called it impractical. It has since rescued many people from sudden death.

questions.q: The face of the Resusci Anne CPR doll came from the death mask of?
questions.a: An unidentified young woman found in the Seine
w: A nurse from World War I
questions.e: L’Inconnue de la Seine. Often called the most-kissed face in the world, and nobody ever learned her name.

questions.q: The landmark 1960 JAMA paper on closed-chest cardiac massage was led by William Kouwenhoven, who was trained as?
questions.e: Johns Hopkins, with Jude and Knickerbocker. Sometimes you need someone who doesn’t know it can’t be done.

questions.q: A 2018 study of cardiac arrests in public found bystander CPR was given less often to?
questions.e: About 39% of women against 45% of men, and men were more likely to survive. Researchers are still working out why, and fear of touching a woman’s chest is one suspect.

questions.q: The 2018 PARAMEDIC2 trial found adrenaline in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest improved 30-day survival, but what about good neurological recovery?
questions.e: A small survival gain with no clear gain in brain outcomes. A very uncomfortable result for a very old drug.

questions.q: George Washington died on this date in 1799 after doctors treated a severe throat infection by bloodletting. About how much of his blood did they take?
questions.e: Three doctors attended. The youngest suggested a tracheotomy and was outvoted.

questions.q: The four humours were blood, phlegm, yellow bile and?
questions.e: Greek medicine ran on them for around 2,000 years. Galen was a very convincing man.

questions.q: ‘Melancholy’ literally means?
questions.e: From the Greek ‘melas’ and ‘chole’. A rather dark diagnosis in every sense.

questions.q: Medicinal leeches are still used today, mostly in?
questions.e: They relieve venous congestion in reattached tissue. Their saliva contains hirudin, an anticoagulant. Bloodletting’s last job.

questions.q: The journal The Lancet, founded in 1823, is named after?
questions.a: A sharp tool used for bloodletting
questions.e: Thomas Wakley meant it as a surgical cut through medical nonsense. Also a window, in a nice double meaning.

questions.q: ‘A night with Venus, a lifetime with Mercury’ was a grim saying about the treatment of?
questions.e: The mercury did at least as much damage as the disease, and the rhyme outlived both.

questions.q: Around 1800, London’s Royal Humane Society encouraged rescuers to revive drowning victims by?
questions.a: Blowing tobacco smoke into the rectum
w: Hanging them upside down from a tree
Rolling them on a barrel of rum
Pouring hot oil on the feet
questions.e: Kits were kept along the Thames. Yes, the phrase about blowing smoke does come to mind.

questions.q: In 1898, Bayer began selling which drug as a non-addictive cough medicine?
questions.e: Named from ‘heroisch’, meaning heroic. Heroic marketing, perhaps. Not much else.

questions.q: ‘Hysteria’ comes from the Greek word for?
questions.e: Ancient doctors blamed a wandering womb. Medicine took a very long time to stop finding that plausible.

questions.q: When federal agents tested Clark Stanley’s famous Snake Oil Liniment in 1917, how much snake oil did they find?
questions.e: It was mostly mineral oil, with beef fat and red pepper. Honestly, we’re all a bit disappointed.

questions.q: Today is Zamenhof Day. L.L. Zamenhof, who invented Esperanto, trained as a doctor specialising in?
questions.e: A Warsaw ophthalmologist who dreamed of people understanding each other, and also of seeing each other clearly.

questions.q: What is the leading cause of blindness worldwide?
questions.e: And the surgery to fix it takes about 15 minutes. Access, not technology, is the problem.

questions.q: Which part of the eye is the most commonly transplanted tissue?
questions.e: The eye’s clear front window, and one of transplant’s oldest success stories, going back to 1905.

questions.q: Fred Hollows, famous for his work on avoidable blindness in Aboriginal communities and beyond, was born in?
questions.e: Australia happily claims him anyway, and he’s buried in Bourke. His low-cost lenses changed cataract surgery in Nepal and Eritrea.

questions.q: Which infection is the world’s leading infectious cause of blindness?
questions.e: Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. Repeated infections turn the eyelashes inwards. Many countries have now eliminated it.

questions.q: ‘Pupil’ comes from the Latin for?
questions.e: Look into someone’s eye and you see a tiny reflection of yourself. Romantic, then, and quite creepy.

questions.q: People with severe vision loss who see vivid silent hallucinations while knowing they aren’t real have?
questions.e: Bonnet described his own grandfather in 1760. It’s common and not a sign of mental illness, which many people are relieved to hear.

questions.q: On Pingelap atoll in Micronesia, about 1 in 12 people have?
questions.e: Traced to a typhoon that left only about 20 survivors around 1775. Oliver Sacks wrote about it in ‘The Island of the Colorblind’.

questions.q: Patricia Bath, the first African American woman doctor to receive a medical patent, invented the Laserphaco probe for?
questions.e: She also coined ‘community ophthalmology’ after noticing how much more blindness there was in Harlem.

questions.q: The classic letter chart in the doctor’s office is named after which Dutch eye doctor?
questions.e: From 1862. Those letters are designed to a precise grid, and no, you can’t memorise your way out of it. People try.

questions.q: Today is Beethoven’s likely birthday. Contralto Caroline Unger is said to have turned him round to see the applause he couldn’t hear at the premiere of?
questions.e: Vienna, 1824. It’s a story that’s been polished by years of retelling, but nobody wants to give it up.

questions.q: A 2023 DNA study of locks of Beethoven’s hair found what about the cause of his deafness?
questions.e: It did find hepatitis B and a strong risk of liver disease. The deafness kept its secret.

questions.q: Otosclerosis causes hearing loss mainly by fixing which bone in place?
questions.e: A sticky footplate. Women are affected more, and it can get worse in pregnancy.

questions.q: Which two bedside tests use a 512 Hz tuning fork to check hearing?
questions.e: Between them, they separate conductive loss from sensorineural loss. Very cheap, surprisingly clever.

questions.q: Under WHO’s 2021 grading, normal hearing means thresholds below about?
questions.e: About 1.5 billion people live with some hearing loss. WHO says it’s going up.

questions.q: Orthopaedic surgeon Tony Cicoria developed a sudden passion for piano and composing after?
questions.e: Hit through a payphone in 1994. Sacks tells the story in ‘Musicophilia’.

questions.q: British musician Clive Wearing was left with a memory of only seconds after an infection in 1985, yet could still conduct. What was the infection?
questions.e: His love for his wife Deborah also survived. A striking example of how musical memory lives apart.

questions.q: Scottish percussionist Evelyn Glennie, profoundly deaf since about age 12, is known for playing?
questions.e: She describes hearing as a form of touch, and has Grammys to show for it.

questions.q: Lifelong trouble with recognising tunes or pitch, despite normal hearing, is called?
questions.e: What your uncle has at karaoke is probably a lack of practice. Only a small minority truly have it.

questions.q: In Sydney in 1941, Norman Gregg noticed many babies with cataracts, and went on to link them to which infection in pregnancy?
questions.e: Hearing loss turned out to be part of the picture too. It’s why children are now vaccinated. Mothers’ memories gave him the first clue.

questions.q: On this date in 1903 at Kitty Hawk, Orville Wright’s first powered flight lasted about?
questions.e: Less time than most people spend finding their boarding pass.

questions.q: Wilbur Wright died in 1912 of which infection?
questions.e: Orville had nearly died of it in 1896, with Wilbur nursing him while reading up on flight.

questions.q: In aviation medicine, ‘time of useful consciousness’ is?
questions.a: How long you can act sensibly after losing oxygen
w: The length of a pilot’s duty period
How long you can stay awake on a long-haul flight
The time to recover after a faint
questions.e: At 40,000 feet, it’s only about 15 to 20 seconds. Hence those masks.

questions.q: A 2013 NEJM study of in-flight medical emergencies found the most common problem was?
questions.e: Over a third of the calls. And often a doctor was already on board, pretending to read.

questions.q: Divers are told to wait before flying, mainly to avoid?
questions.e: Lower pressure in the cabin can bring nitrogen bubbles out of solution. It’s an unwise way to end a holiday.

questions.q: Who is regarded as the father of aviation medicine, for his 1878 book on barometric pressure?
questions.e: He showed low oxygen, not low pressure itself, caused the trouble. Two balloonists died in 1875 before his warning reached them.

questions.q: Airline crew get a higher yearly dose of?
questions.e: Less atmosphere overhead, less shielding. It’s why crew are counted as radiation workers in some countries.

questions.q: The WHO project that studied blood clot risk on flights was named after the Wrights: WRIGHT. It found that after a flight over 4 hours the risk of a clot roughly?
questions.e: WHO Research Into Global Hazards of Travel. The absolute risk remains low. That is one very committed acronym.

questions.q: Mae Jemison, the first African American woman in space, was also trained as a?
questions.e: She had also worked for the Peace Corps in Sierra Leone and Liberia. Her CV makes everyone else’s look thin.

questions.q: US Air Force doctor John Stapp famously rode a rocket sled to test?
questions.a: How much deceleration a person could survive
w: Whether pilots could stay awake at speed
questions.e: 46.2 G in 1954, with damage to his eyes and wrists. He also pushed hard for car seatbelts.

questions.q: Today is International Migrants Day. Roughly how many people worldwide live outside the country they were born in?
questions.e: About 300 million people. Many are the workers and carers health systems rely on.

questions.q: New migrants often arrive healthier than people born in their new country. This is known as?
questions.e: The advantage tends to fade with time, as diets, stress and access to care catch up.

questions.q: Which year’s UN convention still gives the global legal definition of a refugee?
questions.e: Written after World War II, with a 1967 protocol extending it around the globe.

questions.q: Interferon-gamma release assays are often used to screen new arrivals for latent TB because, unlike skin tests, they?
questions.a: Aren’t confused by past BCG vaccination
w: Treat the infection at the same time
questions.e: Many people from high-TB countries have had BCG. Blood test, one visit.

questions.q: Which roundworm can keep reinfecting the same person for decades, and turn dangerous if they’re given steroids?
questions.e: Autoinfection is its unusual trick. That’s why people from endemic regions may be tested before immune-suppressing treatment.

questions.q: A person who moved from a malarial region months ago has a fever. Which malaria species can hide in the liver and relapse long after?
questions.e: Hypnozoites, the sleeping liver stage. Ovale can do it too. Falciparum tends not to wait around.

questions.q: Chagas disease, found in Latin American migrants worldwide, is spread by?
questions.e: Named for Brazilian doctor Carlos Chagas, who in 1909 described the bug, the parasite and the disease all at once.

questions.q: Ellis Island doctors used a buttonhook to turn back immigrants’ eyelids, looking for?
questions.e: A diagnosis could mean being sent straight back. A very brisk exam with lifelong consequences.

questions.q: Mary Mallon, an Irish immigrant cook in New York, was held in isolation for about 26 years for carrying which infection?
questions.e: Healthy carriers were barely understood. Her story raises hard questions about stigma as well as hygiene.

questions.q: A new arrival has no vaccination records. Guidelines generally advise?
questions.a: Assume they’re unvaccinated and start catch-up doses
w: Wait until records can be found
Do nothing if they feel well
questions.e: Extra doses are generally safe. Being unprotected is the bigger risk.

questions.q: ‘A Christmas Carol’ was published on this date in 1843. In 1992, a paediatric nephrologist proposed Tiny Tim’s illness was?
questions.e: Donald Lewis also suggested rickets, and that treatment affordable to Scrooge’s money would have helped. No word on the goose.

questions.q: Which scientist’s 1919 work with dogs showed cod liver oil prevented rickets?
questions.e: McCollum then named the factor vitamin D a few years later. The dogs were kept indoors, like many city children.

questions.q: Scrooge first blames Marley’s ghost on?
questions.e: ‘There’s more of gravy than of grave about you.’ A very early case of attributing visions to indigestion.

questions.q: Which modern syndrome takes its name from Joe, the always-sleepy boy in an early Dickens novel?
questions.e: Now called obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Burwell’s 1956 paper had a literary flourish that stuck.

questions.q: Women working in Victorian match factories could develop ‘phossy jaw’, from exposure to?
questions.e: It killed bone in the jaw. London’s matchgirls went on strike at Bryant and May in 1888.

questions.q: Percivall Pott in 1775 made one of the first links between a job and a cancer. Which workers were affected?
questions.e: Soot and scrotal cancer, in men who had climbed chimneys as boys. Grim, even for the time.

questions.q: Who wrote the 1842 ‘Report on the Sanitary Condition of the Labouring Population of Great Britain’?
questions.e: Clean water, drains and a very long-running battle with London’s smell.

questions.q: Godfrey’s Cordial, a Victorian soothing syrup often given to babies, contained?
questions.e: Sold to working mothers who had no other childcare. It kept babies very quiet indeed, and sometimes far worse.

questions.q: Bright green ‘Scheele’s Green’ wallpaper, fashionable in Victorian homes, contained?
questions.e: The damp could make it give off toxic fumes. William Morris made a fortune from the stuff and dismissed the fuss.

questions.q: In 1858, Charles Dickens gave a famous fundraising speech that saved which London hospital?
questions.e: Founded in 1852 by Charles West as Britain’s first children’s hospital. Dickens raised a small fortune on the night.

questions.q: Today is International Human Solidarity Day. Which 2008 WHO commission, chaired by Michael Marmot, called for ‘closing the gap in a generation’?
questions.a: Commission on Social Determinants of Health
questions.e: It argued that social injustice was killing people on a grand scale.

questions.q: The Whitehall studies of British civil servants found that illness rates?
questions.a: Rose with each step down the job ladder
questions.e: Even people who were far from poor did worse than those just above them. The gradient is the point.

questions.q: The Preston curve, named after demographer Samuel Preston, shows the relationship between national income and?
questions.e: It rises steeply in poorer countries and then flattens. Money helps most where there’s least of it.

questions.q: Who wrote that ‘medicine is a social science’, after investigating a typhus outbreak in Upper Silesia in 1848?
questions.e: He prescribed democracy, education and freedom for the region. His report wasn’t warmly welcomed.

questions.q: In 1987, Paul Farmer co-founded Partners In Health to bring care to?
questions.e: It later spread worldwide. He insisted that poor patients deserved the same care as anyone else.

questions.q: Médecins Sans Frontières, winner of the 1999 Nobel Peace Prize, was founded in 1971 in?
questions.e: By doctors who wanted freedom to speak out, as well as to treat.

questions.q: Jamaican-born doctor Cicely Williams introduced the Ghanaian word ‘kwashiorkor’ in the 1930s. It’s a form of?
questions.e: From the Ga language, for the illness of the child displaced when a new baby arrives. She later attacked infant formula marketing in her ‘Milk and Murder’ speech.

questions.q: WHO says what share of maternal deaths happen in low and lower-middle-income countries?
questions.e: Almost all preventable, and largely a matter of where a woman happens to live.

questions.q: Te Whare Tapa Whā, Mason Durie’s Māori model of health, compares well-being to?
questions.a: The four walls of a house
questions.e: Physical, mental, family and spiritual walls, standing on the land. A broader view than a blood pressure chart.

questions.q: In 1991, Bernadine Healy, the first woman to lead the US NIH, coined ‘Yentl syndrome’ for?
questions.a: Women’s heart disease being missed unless it looks like men’s
questions.e: Named after the Isaac Bashevis Singer character who dressed as a boy to study. A point well made.

questions.q: Today is World Meditation Day. ‘Rest and digest’ is the job of which part of the nervous system?
questions.e: The vagus nerve does most of the work here. A bit like you, on your sofa.

questions.q: Cortisol, the body’s main stress hormone, comes from the?
questions.e: It has a useful daily rhythm, and is not, as your wellness app insists, a villain.

questions.q: Who coined the phrase ‘fight or flight’ in the early 20th century?
questions.e: Selye came along later with the word ‘stress’. Nobody got to coin ‘freeze’.

questions.q: Mindfulness-based stress reduction was developed in 1979 at the University of Massachusetts by?
questions.e: Eight weeks, a lot of sitting. A molecular biologist by training, as it happens.

questions.q: ‘Box breathing’ means breathing in, holding, breathing out and holding for?
questions.e: Usually a count of four each. Popular in the military, and in dreadful meetings.

questions.q: Which sleep stage, identified by Eugene Aserinsky in 1953, is the one most linked to vivid dreams?
questions.e: He discovered it studying his own 8-year-old son. Kleitman, his supervisor, got much of the fame.

questions.q: A 2004 study by Elissa Epel and Elizabeth Blackburn found that women under long-term stress caring for sick children had shorter?
questions.e: Cellular ageing that seemed to track with how much stress they felt, not just with how long they’d been caring.

questions.q: After hours on a block-stacking game, people see falling shapes as they drop off to sleep. This is called the?
questions.e: Named after the most obvious offender. Even people with amnesia who forgot playing have reported it.

questions.q: The sudden jolt you sometimes get just as you fall asleep is called a?
questions.e: Very common and harmless, and it isn’t your body worried that you’re falling off a tree. Well, probably not.

questions.q: Heart rate rising on the in-breath and falling on the out-breath is normal, and called?
questions.e: It’s strongest in young, fit people. Slow breathing makes it more pronounced, which is partly the point.

questions.q: Today is Ramanujan’s birthday. The Indian maths genius died in 1920, aged 32, and his illness, long blamed on TB, is now thought more likely to have been?
questions.e: D.A.B. Young’s 1994 review argued for hepatic amoebiasis, caught years earlier in India and very treatable by then.

questions.q: Visiting Ramanujan in hospital, G.H. Hardy mentioned his taxi’s dull number. Ramanujan said it was the smallest sum of two cubes in two ways. What was it?
questions.e: Now called the taxicab number. Doctors have never found a way to answer a colleague like that on rounds.

questions.q: The number needed to treat is 1 divided by?
questions.e: If a drug drops risk from 5% to 3%, the absolute reduction is 2%, so you treat 50 people for one to benefit.

questions.q: William Gosset published the t-test as ‘Student’ because which employer banned staff from publishing?
questions.e: Statistics, brought to you by stout. Small samples of barley needed careful maths.

questions.q: A Type II error is?
questions.a: A false negative: missing a real effect
questions.e: Type I sees things that aren’t there. Type II misses what is.

questions.q: The conventional threshold for ‘statistical significance’ is a p-value below?
questions.e: Ronald Fisher suggested it as a convenient choice in the 1920s, not as a law of nature.

questions.q: A test’s sensitivity is the proportion of?
questions.a: People with the disease who test positive
w: People without the disease who test negative
questions.e: A highly sensitive test, if negative, helps rule the disease out. Your examiners will insist.

questions.q: A drug cuts a risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. That’s a relative reduction of 50%. The absolute reduction is?
questions.e: Headlines prefer the first figure. Be suspicious of big numbers and small denominators.

questions.q: In a normal distribution, about 95% of values fall within how many standard deviations of the mean?
questions.e: About 68% are within one. A very tidy bell, but real patients rarely read the textbook.

questions.q: In 1858, who became the first woman elected to the Royal Statistical Society?
questions.e: Her diagrams made politicians understand mortality rates. Some of them, anyway.

questions.q: On this date in 1954, the first successful kidney transplant took place in Boston, led by?
questions.e: Ronald Herrick gave a kidney to his identical twin Richard. Murray later won a Nobel Prize.

questions.q: Willem Kolff built the first working dialysis machine in the occupied Netherlands, using membranes made from?
questions.e: With orange juice cans and a washing-machine part. In 1945, a 67-year-old woman, Sofia Schafstadt, became his first patient to survive.

questions.q: In the 1960s, a Seattle committee of mostly non-doctors became notorious for deciding?
questions.e: A 1962 Life magazine story called them the people who decide who lives and who dies. Often cited as a starting point for modern bioethics.

questions.q: Ciclosporin, which changed transplant medicine, was found in a fungus from soil collected in?
questions.e: A Sandoz employee on holiday brought home the sample. Always pack a soil bag, kids.

questions.q: Hyperacute rejection, within minutes or hours of a transplant, is caused by?
w: T cells taking days to activate
questions.e: Careful cross-matching means surgeons rarely see this any more. Surgeons don’t miss it.

questions.q: Tacrolimus and ciclosporin belong to which drug class?
questions.e: They stop T cells getting their marching orders. Tacrolimus came from Japanese soil near Mount Tsukuba.

questions.q: When a kidney is transplanted, what normally happens to the person’s own kidneys?
w: Only the left one is removed
questions.e: So many transplant recipients have three kidneys. The new one usually goes in the groin area, near the iliac vessels.

questions.q: Economist Alvin Roth won a 2012 Nobel Prize partly for work on?
questions.e: Paired kidney exchange lets incompatible pairs swap. A rare Nobel where the economics saves lives directly.

questions.q: Which country has for many years led the world in deceased organ donation rates?
questions.e: An opt-out law helps, but a well-organised network of transplant coordinators is the real secret.

questions.q: In March 2024, a Boston hospital transplanted a genetically edited kidney from which animal into a living man?
questions.e: A world first in a living patient. Xenotransplant research is moving quickly, and pigs are not asked for their opinion.

theme: Joules, and the night before Christmas

questions.q: James Joule, born on this date in 1818 and honoured by the unit of energy, was by trade a?
questions.e: He did his precise heat experiments in the family brewery, where accurate thermometers mattered.

questions.q: One kilocalorie is equal to about how many kilojoules?
questions.e: Handy for comparing a mince pie to anything at all on a label from Australia.

questions.q: Which of these contains about 29 kJ per gram, more than carbs or protein?
questions.e: Second only to fat, at about 37 kJ per gram. The festive punch has a lot to answer for.

questions.q: For most adults, the largest share of daily energy use goes on?
questions.e: Around 60 to 75%. And no, the Christmas crossword doesn’t count as a workout.

questions.q: Brown fat makes heat using a protein called?
questions.e: It lets protons bypass ATP production and burn fuel for warmth. Also known as thermogenin.

questions.q: Elsie Widdowson’s work with Robert McCance on wartime diets led Britain to add what to bread in World War II?
questions.e: They tested rations on themselves first. Their book ‘The Composition of Foods’ became the dietitian’s bible.

questions.q: Why are button batteries such a risk if swallowed, especially at Christmas?
questions.a: They can burn through the oesophagus within hours
w: They block the bowel for months
They release mercury into the blood
questions.e: Burns can begin within about 2 hours. They’re in a lot of toys, cards and remote controls this time of year.

questions.q: ‘Holiday heart syndrome’, first described by Philip Ettinger in 1978, is an arrhythmia after?
questions.e: Often atrial fibrillation. The tinsel is not to blame.

questions.q: A 2018 BMJ study from Sweden found heart attack risk peaked around which occasion and time?
questions.e: Up 37%, on a Swedish register of nearly 300,000 cases. A busy night for cardiologists, and not only Santa.

questions.q: Blaming the turkey’s tryptophan for your post-Christmas lunch sleep is?
questions.a: A myth: turkey has no more than many other meats
w: True: turkey has by far the most
True, but only for dark meat
questions.e: Blame the big meal, the wine and the relatives instead.

questions.q: Clara Barton, born on Christmas Day in 1821, founded which organisation in 1881?
questions.e: The ‘Angel of the Battlefield’ had also run a missing soldiers’ office. She kept on working until she was 83.

questions.q: The Red Cross itself grew out of Henry Dunant’s horror at the aftermath of which 1859 battle?
questions.e: His book led to the Geneva Convention. He then shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

questions.q: Christmas disease, or haemophilia B, is a lack of which clotting factor?
questions.e: Named after the patient, Stephen Christmas. The paper, led by Rosemary Biggs, ran in the BMJ’s Christmas issue in 1952. Someone had a sense of timing.

questions.q: Myotonic dystrophy classically gives what kind of eye finding?
questions.e: Tiny multicoloured crystals that twinkle on the slit lamp. A memorable name for a useful clue.

questions.q: Which festive plant has a fearsome reputation, but in reality usually causes only mild stomach upset?
questions.e: Keep kids away from holly and mistletoe berries. The poinsettia, however, has been slandered for a century.

questions.q: Mary Breckinridge founded the Frontier Nursing Service in 1925, sending nurse-midwives through rural Kentucky on?
questions.e: Maternal deaths among their patients fell far below the national rate. Not bad for a service that ran on oats.

questions.q: The word ‘midwife’ comes from Old English meaning?
questions.e: ‘Mid’ meant with. A job description that’s stayed good for a thousand years.

questions.q: After being told by the War Office to ‘go home and sit still’, Scottish doctor Elsie Inglis set up which World War I organisation?
questions.e: Its all-female teams served in France, Serbia and Russia. The War Office has rarely looked so silly.

questions.q: In 1879, Mary Eliza Mahoney became the first African American to?
questions.a: Complete professional nurse training in the US
w: Earn a medical degree in the US
Graduate from nursing school in Britain
questions.e: At the New England Hospital for Women and Children in Boston. Only 4 of her class of 42 made it through.

questions.q: According to a 2012 BMJ Christmas paper, why might Rudolph’s nose be red?
questions.a: A very dense network of tiny blood vessels
questions.e: They studied reindeer noses with a video microscope. It’s peer-reviewed, and yes, it’s real.

questions.q: The Curies announced radium on 26 December 1898, after extracting it from tonnes of which ore?
questions.e: Hauled by the bag and stirred by Marie in a leaky shed. The Boxing Day sales had nothing on her.

questions.q: The 1920s ‘Radium Girls’ took in radium in their factory jobs by?
questions.e: Told it was safe, they painted watch dials and sometimes even their nails. Bosses knew better. Five of them sued.

questions.q: Why did radium end up in the jawbones and skeletons of those exposed?
w: It’s attracted to iron in the bone
questions.e: Same column of the periodic table. Bone has trouble telling them apart.

questions.q: Wealthy American golfer Eben Byers died in 1932 after years of drinking which radium health tonic?
questions.e: ‘The radium water worked fine until his jaw came off,’ noted the Wall Street Journal. The FDA got a lot more interested.

questions.q: Marie Curie died in 1934 from?
questions.e: Almost certainly due to her years around radiation. Her notebooks are still radioactive, and kept in lead-lined boxes.

questions.q: Which element did the Curies name after Marie’s homeland?
questions.e: Named in 1898, when Poland didn’t officially exist on the map. A bit of chemistry with a political edge.

questions.q: Irène Joliot-Curie, Marie’s daughter, won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, with her husband Frédéric, for?
questions.e: Two generations, five Nobel Prizes in the family. Dinner must have been something.

questions.q: The 1987 Goiânia accident in Brazil, in which people were drawn to a strange blue glow from an abandoned radiotherapy machine, involved?
questions.e: Four people died, including a six-year-old girl, and thousands needed checking. One of the worst radiological accidents in history.

questions.q: Which New Jersey medical examiner both investigated the Radium Girls and, in 1928, gave boxing’s ‘punch drunk’ its medical description?
questions.e: A Boxing Day nod for you. He took both groups seriously when their employers would not.

questions.q: Radium-223 is used today to treat?
questions.e: Its bone-seeking trick is finally put to good use. A century on, radium turned out to be useful after all.

questions.q: Today is International Day of Epidemic Preparedness. The basic reproduction number (R0) for measles is usually quoted as?
questions.e: One of the most contagious infections known. Hence the high vaccination target.

questions.q: If a disease has an R0 of 5, the herd immunity threshold is about?
questions.e: That’s 1 − 1/R0. Maths that kept measles out of many a country.

questions.q: Quarantine began in the Adriatic port of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) in 1377, at first using an isolation period of?
questions.e: Venice stretched it to 40, or ‘quaranta giorni’, which is where we got the word.

questions.q: In 1975, Rahima Banu, a young girl in Bangladesh, became known for what?
questions.a: The last naturally occurring case of variola major smallpox
w: The first polio vaccine recipient in Asia
The first recorded case of avian flu
The last case of guinea worm in Asia
questions.e: She survived. Her case marked the end of the most deadly form of one of humanity’s oldest killers.

questions.q: After smallpox, which disease became the second ever to be declared eradicated, in 2011?
questions.e: A cattle plague that had ravaged farmers and herders for centuries. Polio is taking its time.

questions.q: Which British statistician’s 1965 criteria, including strength, consistency and temporality, still help judge whether something causes disease?
questions.e: Nine ‘viewpoints’, as he called them. He did not intend them to be a tick-box. Everyone uses them as a tick-box.

questions.q: Janet Lane-Claypon, an often overlooked pioneer, developed which two study designs in the early 20th century?
questions.e: Looking at feeding in babies and later breast cancer. Then she had to give up her career after marrying, under civil service rules.

questions.q: Who was the Congolese scientist who took the first samples in the 1976 Ebola outbreak, and has been a leader in the fight ever since?
questions.e: He went to the village of Yambuku, then in Zaire, and later led development of the ebola antibody treatment mAb114.

questions.q: Which WHO doctor raised the alarm about SARS in Hanoi in 2003, before dying of it himself?
questions.e: An Italian infectious disease specialist. He persuaded Vietnam to act fast, which helped save many lives.

questions.q: The classic SIR epidemic model of 1927 was developed by?
questions.e: Susceptible, infected, recovered. A surprisingly simple set of equations that still gets a workout.

questions.q: Today is Stan Lee’s birthday. In Marvel comics, Bruce Banner became the Hulk after exposure to?
questions.e: In reality, radiation causes burns and cancer risk, not green muscle. Please don’t try.

questions.q: Highly superior autobiographical memory, or hyperthymesia, was first described in 2006 in?
questions.e: She can recall almost every day of her life since she was a teenager. It isn’t always a gift, she says.

questions.q: A person who sees letters and numbers in particular colours has a form of?
questions.e: Grapheme-colour is the most common kind. Your 7 is yellow? Theirs may be blue, and they’re quite sure.

questions.q: Which gene, when inactive, gives Belgian Blue cattle and one rare German boy unusually big muscles?
questions.e: Myostatin normally limits muscle growth. A boy described in 2004 had very large muscles from birth.

questions.q: Robert Wadlow, the tallest person in recorded history, grew to about 2.72 m because of?
questions.a: Too much growth hormone from his pituitary
questions.e: Before growth plates close, too much growth hormone means gigantism. He was known for his kindness, too.

questions.q: The Bajau ‘sea nomads’ of South-East Asia, who are renowned for long free dives, have been found to have larger?
questions.e: The spleen releases extra red cells. A gene variant behind this has been traced by scientists. Aquaman, take note.

questions.q: Jo Cameron, a Scottish woman who feels almost no pain and heals quickly, was found in 2019 to have a mutation in a gene nicknamed?
questions.e: Yes, that’s the real name. She only learned how unusual she was in her sixties, and scientists hope it can lead to new pain treatments.

questions.q: Daniel Kish, who has been blind from infancy, is famous for navigating by?
questions.a: Clicking his tongue and using echoes
w: Feeling air pressure on his face
questions.e: ‘Human echolocation’, which he teaches. Daredevil had to be hit by radioactive waste to do it.

questions.q: Having four types of colour-sensing cone, instead of the usual three, is called tetrachromacy and has been found in?
questions.e: Linked to the X chromosome, so women get two chances. They may see colours most of us just can’t.

questions.q: Which human organ can regrow after large parts of it are removed, like Wolverine?
questions.e: Living donors can give part of it, and it grows back within months. The Greeks seem to have noticed in the story of Prometheus.

questions.q: Today is Charles Goodyear’s birthday. Vulcanisation, the process he found, involves heating rubber with?
questions.e: A lucky spill on a hot stove, according to the legend. He died in debt.

questions.q: Natural latex comes from which tree?
questions.e: From the Amazon, famously smuggled to Asian plantations in the 1870s.

questions.q: Caroline Hampton, the nurse who became William Halsted’s wife, is the reason surgical rubber gloves exist. Why?
w: She needed a better grip on instruments
questions.e: Goodyear made her some thin ones. The romance wrote itself, and everyone else followed later.

questions.q: People with latex allergy may also react to which fruits?
questions.e: Latex-fruit syndrome. The proteins look similar, and the immune system isn’t fussy.

questions.q: Which group has historically had an especially high rate of latex allergy, because of repeated surgery and catheter use?
questions.e: Many hospitals now go latex-free in their care, which has made a real difference.

questions.q: What keeps a Foley catheter in the bladder?
questions.e: Boston surgeon Frederic Foley gave his name to it in the 1930s, and his name now comes up every day on a ward somewhere.

questions.q: Before rubber arrived, condoms in Europe were often made from?
questions.e: Goodyear’s process led to rubber condoms in the 1850s. They were reusable. Please let that sink in.

questions.q: Which device, invented by British anaesthetist Archie Brain in the 1980s, sits over the larynx to keep the airway open?
questions.e: He made the early prototypes himself. A rare modern invention that changed anaesthesia everywhere.

questions.q: The contraceptive diaphragm, made from rubber or silicone, is designed to cover?
questions.e: A big step forward for women’s choice in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

questions.q: Tight rubber bands placed by a doctor are a common treatment for?
questions.e: The tissue withers and falls off within a week or so. Not quite how you’d want to use your office supplies.

theme: Back in the game: sports medicine

questions.q: Today is Tiger Woods’s birthday. He won the 2019 Masters less than two years after surgery on his?
questions.e: A spinal fusion in 2017, then his 15th major title. Few had seen that coming.

questions.q: Golfer’s elbow is pain at the?
questions.e: Tennis elbow gets the outside. Most sufferers have played neither, which rather spoils the naming.

questions.q: The Ottawa ankle rules help decide?
questions.a: Whether an ankle injury needs an X-ray
questions.e: Cut needless X-rays while missing almost no fractures. A small victory for common sense.

questions.q: Non-contact ACL tears occur several times more often in which group of athletes?
questions.e: Football and basketball show it most clearly. Research into why, and training to prevent it, is finally catching up.

questions.q: Which bedside test is the classic for spotting an ACL tear?
questions.e: McMurray is for meniscus. Thompson is for the Achilles. Phalen is for the wrist, and you’re in the wrong room.

questions.q: Which surgery, first done on a baseball pitcher in 1974, reconstructs the elbow’s ulnar collateral ligament?
questions.e: Frank Jobe was the surgeon. Pitcher John played another 14 seasons, and now it’s practically a rite of passage.

questions.q: In the ‘PEACE & LOVE’ injury advice, what does the first E stand for?
questions.e: Protect, Elevate, Avoid anti-inflammatories, Compress, Educate. A rethink of RICE, and it’s harder to spell.

questions.q: Which Nigerian-American pathologist first described CTE in a former American football player, in 2005?
questions.e: Mike Webster’s brain. The NFL wasn’t happy. Will Smith played Omalu in ‘Concussion’.

questions.q: The IOC’s term RED-S, introduced in 2014, stands for?
questions.e: It broadened the female athlete triad, recognising that men can be affected too.

questions.q: Roger Bannister, first to run a mile in under four minutes, in 1954, went on to a career as a?
questions.e: He said his medical work mattered more than the mile. Runners remain unconvinced.

theme: Up all night: Boerhaave and New Year

questions.q: Herman Boerhaave, born on this date in 1668, described the oesophageal rupture named after him in 1724, in?
questions.e: Baron van Wassenaer feasted, vomited and died. It remains a poor way to round off a big dinner.

questions.q: Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness oesophageal tear. A Mallory-Weiss tear is?
questions.a: A mucosal tear, usually less serious
w: A tear in the stomach only
A tear in the vocal cords
The same thing, in a younger person
questions.e: Mallory-Weiss usually settles on its own. Boerhaave’s is one of the great surgical emergencies.

questions.q: Mackler’s triad of Boerhaave syndrome is vomiting, lower chest pain and?
questions.e: Air under the skin of the neck. Only a minority have all three, so the suspicious doctor wins.

questions.q: Boerhaave was famous for bringing students to the bedside at which Dutch university?
questions.e: Students came from all over Europe, and modern clinical teaching owes him a lot. Letters addressed to him simply as ‘Boerhaave, Europe’ supposedly arrived.

questions.q: Alcohol’s first breakdown product, often blamed for flushing and hangovers, is?
questions.e: Nastier than the alcohol itself. Your liver’s doing its best, truly.

questions.q: The medical name for a hangover, proposed in a 2000 paper, is?
questions.e: From a Norwegian word for uneasiness after debauchery, and the Greek for pain. Now you can say it with a straight face at work tomorrow.

questions.q: About a third of East Asian people carry a variant of which enzyme gene, causing the ‘alcohol flush’?
questions.e: Acetaldehyde builds up. It also raises the risk of oesophageal cancer in those who drink, so the flush is a good warning.

questions.q: Heavy drinkers are given which vitamin to protect against Wernicke encephalopathy?
questions.e: Confusion, trouble with eye movements and unsteady walking. Easy to miss, and serious.

questions.q: Alcohol makes you urinate more because it suppresses which hormone?
questions.e: The queue for the bathroom at midnight is pure endocrinology.

questions.q: Which chronic vomiting syndrome is classically relieved by long hot showers?
questions.e: Hot showers ease it for a while. Stopping long-term heavy cannabis use is what actually fixes it. Happy New Year.
